note: Solomon, the son of David—a king who asked God for wisdom instead of riches, and God gave him both. These are his collected words, meant to be handed down. When you read what follows, you're sitting with one of the wisest men who ever lived.

Notice the pairing: wisdom and instruction, words and understanding. They go together. You don't get one without sitting with the other. This is why we need teachers and books—not to replace thinking, but to sharpen it.

Wise dealing, righteousness, justice, equity—these aren't abstract. They're how you treat the people in front of you: fair, honest, honoring what's right even when it costs. The Lord cares about how you spend your Monday morning.

Prudence to the simple, knowledge to the young—Solomon isn't writing only for the clever. He's reaching for ordinary people just starting out, giving them tools before they stumble into the ditch. That's the heart of a good teacher.

Even the wise keep listening. The man of understanding stays hungry to learn more. I've watched people grow old either because they kept that thirst alive or because they thought they already knew enough. The difference shows in their faces.

Proverbs, parables, riddles—the wise teach in stories and questions, not just commands. They make you think. That's why a single verse can wake you up differently on two different mornings in your life.

The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge—not the end, the beginning. It's the door. When you step through it, you start to see what the world is really like. Foolishness is ignoring that door and trusting your own eye instead.

Both father and mother—your parents together were meant to shape you. Some of us didn't have that gift, but we can look for wisdom-keepers, older voices who love us enough to speak hard truth. The Lord supplies what we're missing if we're listening.
A garland for your head, chains around your neck—ornaments, beauty, dignity. Good teaching makes you stand taller. It's not burden; it's adornment. You're graced by it, not trapped.

The temptation to run with sinners—it never stops coming, just wears different faces at different seasons. The answer stays the same: don't consent. Don't give your nod. Don't let yourself believe 'this time is different.'

Notice how smooth they make it sound—'come with us.' Temptation always sounds like friendship and shared purpose. These men dress up violence as if it were a business venture. That's how sin sells itself.

Sheol, the pit—they're invoking the underworld itself, comparing their appetite to death. These aren't ordinary criminals; they're consumed by greed so total they don't see the innocent as human anymore. That's where hatred goes when it grows unchecked.

All valuable wealth, all plunder—they promise abundance. That's the bait every temptation uses. But notice: it never brings what it promises, only what it threatens. The house fills, but the soul stays empty.

One purse among them all—they want you to blur the line between yourself and the group. Once you're in, you're responsible. That's the trap. They're not offering partnership; they're asking for complicity.
Don't walk on the path with them, keep your foot from it—distance is mercy. The simplest wisdom sometimes is just turning away before the argument starts. Not every voice deserves a debate.

Their feet run to evil, hurry to shed blood—notice the speed. Evil wants urgency; it wants you moving fast so you don't think. Whenever something pushes hard and won't wait, that's a signal to stop and pray.

In vain is the net spread in sight of any bird—the bird sees the trap. Here's the truth these men miss: they're not as clever as they think. The Lord doesn't hide His warnings; He spreads them right out in front of anyone watching.

They lay wait for their own blood—the final irony. The trap they set for others catches them. The very schemes they hatch to destroy the innocent circle back and destroy themselves. That's not luck; that's the shape of a world made by God.

Greed for gain takes away the life of its owners—not eventually, gradually now. Watch a person consumed by the hunger for more, and you see someone hollowed out, never at rest, never at peace. The thing you chase ends up chasing you.

Wisdom calls aloud in the street—she's not hidden in temples or whispered in secret rooms. She's out where the people are, calling for anyone with ears. The Lord makes sure no one can claim they never heard.
At the entrance of the city gates—where decisions were made, where justice was dispensed, where everyone passed through. Wisdom sets herself where she matters most. She knows human nature.

How long will you love simplicity, delight in mockery, hate knowledge?—Wisdom grows impatient. She's been calling. She's tired of waiting for people to choose what's good for them. There's urgency in her voice now, almost exasperation.

Turn at my reproof—one word can change everything. The offer is still open: turn around and I'll pour out my spirit on you. Not punishment, not judgment. Just the pouring out of what you need to live well.

I have called, you have refused; I have stretched out my hand, no one paid attention—the Lord's patience has limits. Not because He's impatient by nature, but because He loves us too much to force grace on someone who keeps saying no.

You have ignored all my counsel and wanted none of my reproof—not selective hearing, but a wholesale refusal. This is the choice that breaks the heart of heaven: the person who knows the way and walks past it anyway.

I will mock when calamity overtakes you—even Wisdom turns away. Not with cruelty, but with sorrow. When you've refused every warning and walked into the pit anyway, there's nothing left but the silence of unanswered calls. That's the loneliness of consequence.

Like a storm, like a whirlwind, distress and anguish—suffering doesn't come politely. When judgment falls on those who refused every gentle call, it comes with force. This is what happens when you run from mercy long enough.

They will seek me diligently, but will not find me—desperation comes too late if it comes after you've spent a lifetime saying no. The door closes. Not because God is cruel, but because real choice means something must be final, or choice means nothing.

They hated knowledge, didn't choose the fear of Yahweh—it was a choice, not an accident. They could have turned their faces toward God and walked toward wisdom. They turned away instead. That turned-away-ness is what they reap.

They despised all my reproof—not just ignored it, but actively despised it. They found wisdom contemptible. When you harden your heart that far, you're not just refusing good counsel; you're calling good evil.

They will eat of the fruit of their own way—not punishment handed down, but the natural harvest of seeds they planted. This is mercy too, in a way: you get to see the truth. What you do matters. It matters eternally.

Looking back from a longer road, I see how often the simple backslide and the careless ease away into destruction—not always dramatically, but steadily. Readers today hear an echo in this verse: how many of us have watched someone we love drift away from what they once knew was true, and nothing could stop them? As of 2026-10, I'm grateful the Lord still calls.

Whoever listens to me will dwell securely—there it is. The choice. Listen and you live at peace, free from the fear of harm because you're under God's care. This is the offer Wisdom has been making all along: not wealth or power, but rest.

The first word is 'My son'—not a command barked from on high, but an invitation from someone who loves you. Notice: receiving and storing. We don't just hear wisdom; we keep it, let it settle into us like a patient teacher's gift.
Turn your ear, apply your heart—two parts of you answering the call. Your ear listens; your heart responds. This is what real learning looks like: the whole person leaning in.
Call out, lift up your voice—wisdom won't creep in quietly. There's urgency here, like someone desperate for water in the desert. The Father hears a sincere cry for understanding.

Seek her as silver, search for her as hidden treasures—ancient wisdom, newly treasured. In time, a prospector might abandon the search if the labor seems fruitless. But here, the seeker persists because wisdom is worth more than anything else. Christ is that treasure the merchant sells all to obtain.

Then you will understand the fear of Yahweh. Notice the word 'then'—it doesn't come first; it's the harvest after the seeking. And 'fear of Yahweh' blooms when we truly know God's character: that He is both perfectly holy and boundlessly kind.

Wisdom comes from His mouth. So it's not something we manufacture or deserve—it's a gift spoken forth by the God who knows all things. When we listen, we're listening to the voice that held creation together.

He lays up sound wisdom for the upright, a shield to those who walk in integrity. The image is beautiful: like a parent storing good provisions for a child, the Lord stores up protection for those who choose the hard, right path.

He guards the paths of justice and preserves the way of His saints. We don't walk these roads alone; the Lord is actively tending them, like a shepherd watching his flock. 'Saints' here means all of us who belong to Him—not heroes, but His beloved.

Then you will understand righteousness and justice, equity and every good path. After all the seeking, the listening, the storing—understanding comes. Not as theory, but as lived knowledge: you can feel the difference between right and wrong, between a path that leads home and one that leads astray.

Wisdom enters your heart, and knowledge becomes pleasant to your soul—a sweetness, not a burden. In the psalms and songs, we see this: truth sets us free because it matches reality, and living in line with how things actually are brings a deep peace. Jesus is that Living Way.

Discretion will watch over you. Understanding will keep you. Two guardians—one watches your steps, the other keeps you safe. It's a promise: when you have wisdom, you're not left to stumble blindly through the dark.

Deliver you from the way of evil, from men who speak perverse things—from voices that twist truth. Wisdom guards you not with a fence, but with the quiet confidence of knowing what's true. You can hear lies now; they don't fool you anymore.

Those who forsake the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness. A choice, not an accident—they turn away. This is the Bible's diagnosis: sin is a door we choose to walk through, even when we know where it leads.

Who rejoice to do evil, delight in perverseness—evil becomes their joy. This is the saddest part: when a human heart has walked so far into darkness that it loves the damage itself. Yet even here, God's patience still waits.

Crooked in their ways, wayward in their paths—the picture is complete. A life turned from wisdom isn't a straight road; it's twisting, unreliable, always bending toward harm. Wisdom keeps you steady; evil keeps you turning.

Deliver you from the strange woman, from the foreigner who flatters with her words. The 'strange woman' is not a person, but a picture of seduction itself—whatever tempts you with smooth words away from your covenant. Wisdom helps you see the trap before you step in.

She forsakes the friend of her youth, forgets the covenant of her God—betrayal and broken promises. Notice the poet links them: when we abandon our covenant with God, we become capable of abandoning the people we love. The roots run deep.

Her house leads down to death, her paths to the departed spirits. Not meant as literal death, but as the slow dying of the soul when you follow enticement instead of truth. The wages of sin, Paul would later write, is death—separation, emptiness, loss.

None who go to her return again, neither do they attain the paths of life. A hard truth, but a true one: some paths, once walked too far, are hard to turn back from. Yet—God's mercy is deeper than even our own despair. Grace still reaches.

That you may walk in the way of good men, keep the paths of the righteous. Here's the fruit: you're no longer alone. Wisdom places you among those who are also seeking, walking, keeping faith. You belong to a company of the faithful.

The upright will dwell in the land. The perfect will remain in it—a promise wrapped in reality. Those who live with integrity build lives that stand; they have roots, inheritance, a place. In Jesus, we find our true home, the land of resurrection, where we remain forever.

The wicked will be cut off from the land. Looking back from a longer road, I see now: this isn't cruelty, but mercy in reverse. The Lord doesn't force the wicked to stay; He lets them go their way, and what they sow, they reap. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful His Word tells us this truth plainly—that choices have consequences, and we're free to choose well.
A father's voice, steady and close: don't let the good words slip away, the ones that shaped you. Let them settle into your heart where they can speak back to you when you most need them.
Long days, full years, deep peace—this is the promise of wisdom kept close. Not the striving kind of long life, but the kind you actually want to live.
Kindness and truth—not two different things, but woven together. Write them where you'll see them every day. The tablet of the heart is where they stay alive.
When kindness and truth are your ornament, people—and God—see you clearly. You'll find yourself welcomed, understood, trusted.
This is the hinge on which everything turns: all your heart to Him, and stop leaning so hard on what you think you know. The weakness here is actually the strength.
Acknowledge Him in the small steps, the daily forks in the road. His work is to straighten the path. Yours is to notice Him there.
The moment we think we've got it figured out is the moment we're already lost. True wisdom bows, fears God, and turns away from what hardens the heart.
There's a wholeness that comes from this kind of humility. It reaches down into the bones, steadies the body, makes the whole self well.
Honor Him with the firstfruits, not the leftovers. Give Him what costs something. This is how we say that He comes first, that He is first.
The barns full, the vats running over—not scarcity or hoarding, but abundance that comes from putting first things first. Generosity that has enough.
The sting of reproof can feel like rejection, but the father's hand is still a father's hand. Don't harden against the voice that calls you back.
Correction is the language of love—the Psalmist knew it, we know it now: the Lord reproves those He loves as a father rejoices over a son He delights in.
Happy—blessed all the way through—the one who finds wisdom, who hunts for it like something precious lost. The happiness is in the finding, in the understanding.
Silver tarnishes, gold can be a burden. But wisdom keeps giving back, keeps working for you, long after the glitter is gone.
More valuable than rubies—not in the marketplace, but to the heart that knows. When you've held both in your hands, you know which one stays beautiful.
Long life and true riches in her hands—not the frantic scrambling kind, but the steady kind that comes from knowing what matters. Honor finds you when you stop chasing it.
Her paths don't demand your exhaustion. They don't offer the cheap thrill of sin. What she offers is pleasantness—the solid peace of a life walking straight.
The tree of life from Eden's garden—and wisdom is that. Hold on to her and you hold on to what gives life. The ancient symbol speaks in every age.
The God who built the cosmos in wisdom—deep, measured, perfect. When you're seeking wisdom, you're seeking to think like the One who made everything.
The depths, the heavens, the dew—His knowledge holds it all together. When the world feels like it's flying apart, remember the One who holds the pieces still.
Keep sound wisdom where you can see it, where it shapes what you do. Discretion—the good judgment to know when and how—is her close companion.
They will be life to your soul—not just information, but sustenance. Grace for your neck, as if a yoke is lifted. This is what wisdom does: it sets you free to live.
Secure steps, steady feet—there's a confidence that comes from knowing you're walking the right way. Not from arrogance, but from trust.
Sweet sleep—the gift to those whose conscience is clear and heart at peace. No thrashing in the dark, no grinding teeth of regret.
Fear will come calling—the panic of sudden crisis, the dread of watching wickedness prosper. But you don't have to answer it. You can choose something else.
Your confidence is His presence, His faithfulness. He guards your steps from the snare. This is the only security worth having.
When you can help and you don't, you've withheld more than a favor. You've withheld the chance to be kind, to be Christ-like. Do it while you can.
"Tomorrow" is the thief of kindness. If you have it now and your neighbor needs it now, the only honest answer is yes, not a deferred promise.
The neighbor trusts you with his peace of mind, his safety. Don't scheme against that trust. A home is only secure when the people in it mean each other well.
Some fights pick themselves; most we choose. Choose differently. The energy spent on pointless strife could go toward something that lasts.

The violent person always looks strong from a distance, and each generation is tempted to admire that strength. But looking back from a longer road, I see now how those paths lead nowhere good. The truly strong are the gentle ones who stand by what's right.
The perverse—the twisted way—turns the Lord's face away, but He turns toward the upright. Which way you go determines which way He looks.
The curse in a wicked house is the Lord stepping back. The blessing in a righteous one is His presence. This is the difference between desolation and home.
The mocker gets what he's looking for—to be seen for his cleverness and contempt. But the humble receive something better: grace. The choice is really that simple.
Wisdom leads to glory, the deep kind that doesn't fade. Foolishness leads somewhere too, but it's a path that ends in its own undoing. The legacy you leave will match the road you walked.

A father is speaking here, and he's not offering clever words—just his instruction. There's a warmth in how he calls them 'sons' and asks them to listen deeply, not just hear. Real wisdom begins when someone stops and truly pays attention.

He's passing on what he himself found trustworthy—'sound learning,' not theories or gossip. The plea not to forsake his law speaks to how easily we drift from what we know is good. He's protecting them, the way someone warns a friend away from a closed door.

Notice his humility here—he's not speaking as someone who had it all figured out. He was tender, an only child, and his parents loved him carefully. He's saying: I was where you are. That makes his next words ring truer.

'Let your heart retain my words'—not your head alone, but the center of who you are. His father knew that real obedience comes from the heart, where it matters. Keeping God's words is how we keep ourselves alive in the deepest sense.

He repeats the call to get wisdom twice—it's not a casual hobby but a serious pursuit. And then, almost sharply: don't forget, don't swerve. He knows how easy it is to abandon what we meant to treasure. The call back is urgent because the drift is real.

Wisdom is personified as 'her'—something we court, love, and honor. The promise is mutual: when we don't abandon her, she doesn't abandon us. When we love her, she keeps us. There's a partnership here, a loyalty that runs both ways.

Wisdom is supreme—not just helpful, not just nice to have, but the thing that towers above all else. And yet the cost is everything you possess. It's an echo of what Jesus said about treasure: sometimes you have to sell all to buy the field. The Lord asks this of us too.
To esteem wisdom, to embrace her—these are acts of honor and love. And the return? Exaltation and honor. The Lord does the same for those who lift Him up: He lifts them higher than they dared hope.

A garland of grace on your head, a crown of splendor—not because you earned them through your own strength, but because you pursued wisdom faithfully. There's beauty in the obedient life, visible and real.
He shifts to a new call—'listen, my son'—and ties it to something we all want: a long life. Not just years, but the years to mean something, to be lived well. That's what his sayings offer.

He's taught in the way of wisdom; he's led in straight paths. There's a gentle confidence in how he speaks—not bragging, but remembering that he's been a faithful guide. A true teacher knows where the pitfalls are because he's walked the safe way.

When you follow the path of wisdom, you move freely—your steps aren't hampered, you don't stumble in the dark. There's a physical ease to right living, a way of walking that feels less clumsy, less afraid.
Instruction becomes like a rope you hold—firm, real, something you grasp and won't release. And why? Because it is your life. Not a decoration or a hobby, but what keeps you alive.

The warning shifts now—don't enter the path of the wicked, don't walk with evil men. He doesn't shame them; he's telling them plainly: there's a direction that leads away from life. Turn away from it.
Avoid it and don't pass by it—the instruction is almost urgent, almost protective. Then turn from it and pass on. There's wisdom in not lingering at the edge of temptation, but simply moving away.

The wicked don't sleep unless they do evil—their minds are restless, their ease depends on harm. It's a portrait of inner torment dressed up as living. There's no peace there, only the hollow satisfaction of causing another to fall.

They eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence—ordinary language for a poisoned life. What they consume nourishes nothing good; it feeds only destruction. The contrast is meant to wake us.

But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, shining more and more until the perfect day—a real image of dawn breaking over the land. The righteous see their way increasingly clear, and there is a day coming when all shadows lift. This light is Jesus Himself.
The wicked walk in darkness and don't know what they stumble over—they're not even aware of their own peril. They move blind. By contrast, the righteous can see.
Another call to attention—attend to my words, turn your ear. The father is asking for his son's full presence. There's something in wise words that only reaches us when we're really listening.
Let them not depart from your eyes—keep them visible, keep remembering. Keep them in the center of your heart—not at the edges where they fade. The words should live where you live.

These words are life and health—not metaphorical, but real nourishment for the whole self. Like bread and water, like breath, wisdom sustains us. Those who find them find what bodies and souls both need.

Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life—readers today hear an echo in this: what we guard in our hearts shapes everything that flows from us. The Lord asks us to tend the inner garden, to let His truth guard our hearts, and the life that springs forth belongs to Him.
Put away a perverse mouth, put corrupt lips far from you—the mouth betrays the heart. If your words are twisted or corrupt, turn away from them. This is practical: stop speaking that way.
Let your eyes look straight ahead, fix your gaze directly before you. There's freedom in a steady gaze—not looking back, not distracted to the sides, but moving forward with clear purpose.
Make the path of your feet level, let all your ways be established—prepare your way, make it firm. This speaks to the life we build by our choices, the foundation we lay with each step.

Don't turn to the right or left, remove your foot from evil—the instruction closes with a call to steadiness and separation. Turn away from what harms, stay on the true path. That's the whole of the father's teaching.
Here the father leans close—pay attention, he says. He knows his son's heart can wander. The Lord speaks to us the same way through His Word, calling us to really *listen*, not just hear.
Discretion and knowledge go together. To keep our lips sealed requires understanding—knowing *why* we guard our words and choices. This is not recklessness but thoughtful faithfulness.
How vividly the proverb paints this: honey on the lips, oil-smooth speech. Sin always advertises itself with sweetness first. The seductive promise is real to the ear, even when what follows is ruin.

The sharp turn from honey to wormwood—from sweet to bitter—shows how quickly pleasure turns to poison when we walk down the wrong path. The Lord teaches us through contrast: this is mercy disguised as warning.
"Her feet go down to death"—unfaithfulness is not a small detour but a descent into Sheol itself. Yet even here, God speaks clearly: turn back. The path downward can still be abandoned.

Notice this: she doesn't even *know* her ways are crooked. Sin blinds us to our own error. This is why we need others to speak truth, and why we must stay in the light rather than prefer the darkness.
"My sons"—plural. The father speaks to all his children, knowing each one faces temptation. And his call is urgent: *listen*. Don't wander. The Lord stands near every listening heart.

"Remove your way far from her." This is not repentance after the fact but prevention before it. Wisdom teaches us to guard the boundary—to not even stand at the door. Fences are placed *before* the cliff.
Your honor, your years—your very life—can be squandered in a moment. The consequences are not just spiritual but real: reputation lost, time wasted, energies given to someone who meant no good.
The tragedy deepens: not only do you suffer, but someone else inherits what you labored for. Your work feeds another's table. This is the hollow echo of wastefulness—you built, but did not keep.
"At your latter end"—old age brings reckoning. The body consumed by disease or years of folly, and the soul with remorse. The Lord grants us time to turn, but it does not last forever.

The bitter admission: I hated instruction. I despised reproof. These words come from someone who once had the chance to listen and refused. This is why wisdom calls us *now*, before regret writes our epitaph.
Teachers, mentors, wise elders—their voices were offered freely, and he stopped his ears. How many of us do the same? The Lord sends His correction through many mouths. Will we listen to any of them?

"Utter ruin, among the gathered assembly"—shame is public. Everyone sees what you became. But even here, there is grace: you're not hidden from God's sight, which means you're not hidden from His mercy either.

The image shifts to wells and cisterns—ancient symbols of life and sustenance. "Your own cistern" speaks to covenant, to boundaries kept sacred. In marriage, fidelity is like drawing from your own living water.
A pointed question: why squander and scatter what is meant to sustain? This applies to marriage but also to every gift—time, talent, affection, faithfulness. We are stewards of what God has given us.
"For yourself alone"—not isolation, but exclusivity within the covenant. What is sacred belongs within the right boundary. The stranger may pass outside, but your heart's spring is reserved for one.

"Let your spring be blessed"—rejoice in your wife of youth. This is not grim duty but delight, a blessing to be grateful for. The father calls his son to *joy*, not mere obedience. This is wisdom speaking about love.

The doe and deer—beautiful creatures, graceful and alive. Here the proverb names love in the body without shame. Captivated by her love, not by lust's cruel trick. There is a difference, and the wise know it.

The father's question cuts to the heart: Why trade the genuine for the counterfeit? Why choose the stranger's embrace when you have been given a covenant partner? This is folly measured against grace.
"Before Yahweh's eyes"—the ancient confession that we are never hidden from God. He sees all our paths. This is not surveillance to condemn but presence to guide. We walk always in His sight.

Readers today hear an echo in these words: the "cords of sin" that bind us—addictions, deceits, habits we cannot shake—still ensnare. Yet Christ breaks every cord. The evil deeds may have held us, but they need not hold us still.
"He will die for lack of instruction." The final word is stark—but it is also a call to life. If you hear this warning now, you need not be him. Wisdom calls; will you answer?

Watch yourself here, child. When you bind yourself with words for another's debt, you've put your own neck on the line. The moment we strike hands in promise, we become answerable—and not just to God, but to the neighbor whose trust we've pledged.
Our words are nets we weave for ourselves. Once spoken, they hold us as surely as they hold anyone listening. This is why I've learned to let hard promises sit a day before I give them.
The Lord sees us in our own snares—and He gives us a way: 'Go, humble yourself.' This word *humble* is the hinge. Pride says defend yourself; humility says go and make it right. See how Jesus moved?
When you're caught in a debt not yours to bear, rest becomes impossible. The psalmist knew this—sleep fled him until he turned back to God. Sometimes our sleeplessness is a mercy, pointing us home.
A gazelle doesn't pause to reason with the hunter. A bird doesn't debate the snare. They flee—swift, instinctive, alive. When you see you're trapped by your own words, don't linger. Move.

The ant teaches what we call 'diligence'—but it's really seeing and responding to what needs doing. The sluggard doesn't move from laziness but from a failure to see. Look at the small faithful thing. Let it wake you.

No chief tells the ant to work. No overseer stands over her with a rod. She labors because the work itself calls, because it matters, because she knows what must be done. This is the freedom the diligent know.
Summer doesn't last, and the ant knows it. She gathers not from greed but from wisdom—from seeing the season and acting while there's time. There's a parable here for every soul I know.

This question is a gentle prod. The sluggard has heard it before and will hear it again—not because God tires of asking, but because each new day is a new chance to wake. How much longer will you choose sleep?

Listen to the music of these words: a little... a little... a little... They sound harmless, small, reasonable. But small compromises gather like frost. One more fold of the hands, and another, and another.

Poverty doesn't creep in. It arrives sudden as a robber, sudden as an armed man. This is what small neglect becomes—not gradually, but all at once. I've seen it. The choice to wake or sleep seems slow until the moment it's not.
A 'worthless person' here isn't someone who failed—it's someone who speaks perverseness as a habit, as an identity. Words shape us. If we let them flow twisted long enough, they twist us.
Watch the small gestures—the wink, the signal, the finger-motion. These are the language of conspiracy, of plans meant to hide. The body speaks what the mouth won't say. Jesus saw through this too.

Perverseness doesn't visit him on occasion. It lives in his heart, plotting always, sowing discord as his daily bread. This is what a heart becomes when it turns from the Lord—endlessly creative at harm.
The Lord breaks such a one suddenly, without remedy. Not as punishment from far away, but as the natural fruit of the path he chose. Sin is patient until it isn't. Then it collapses.

Six things, then seven—a form that says 'and one more, the fullness.' The Lord *hates* these; they are abominations to Him. This list is holy anger, the jealousy of a God who loves what is true and good.
Haughty eyes look down. Lying tongue deceives. Hands that shed innocent blood—these are the tools of pride and cruelty. The Lord lists them because we must see: these are what turn from His image.

A heart that devises evil doesn't stumble into harm—it plots it. And feet swift to mischief: the whole body becomes an instrument of wrong, eager, practiced. This is what refusal of the Lord looks like in motion.

False witness and discord-sower: both break trust itself. One lies under oath; the other fractures brotherhood. Together they destroy the fabric that holds a people together. The Lord hates what unravels His kingdom.

Now the tone shifts. After warning of the perverse, we hear the plea: keep your father's word, don't turn from your mother's teaching. This is how wisdom stays alive—not as abstract truth but as the voice of those who loved you.
Bind them continually on your heart. Tie them around your neck. These aren't metaphors only—they're how you carry what matters most. Worn close, worn daily, until they're part of you.

Readers today hear an echo in this promise: when you walk, the word leads; when you sleep, it guards; when you wake, it speaks. We know this as the peace of conscience, the still small voice, the companionship of truth. How blessed we are to walk held.

The commandment is a lamp, the law is light. Without them, we stumble in darkness, thinking we see. But when we come under this light, our path becomes plain. Every true instruction points us toward life.

The warning here isn't against a woman—it's against being seduced from your path by flattery, by words that promise easy comfort over hard truth. The 'wayward wife's tongue' is any voice that draws you from faithfulness.
Don't lust in your heart—not because beauty is evil, but because lust is the eye before the fall. It turns a person into an object to possess. It closes us to the Lord's will. Guard your heart first.

A prostitute reduces you to bread, a mere commodity. An adulteress hunts your precious life—your soul, your peace, your standing before God. This isn't shame-speaking; it's mercy speaking. Some paths cost everything.

Can a man scoop fire into his lap? The question is rhetorical, spoken to all who think they're exceptions. Fire is fire. Nature is nature. The Lord made the world this way—not to hurt you, but to show that consequences are real.

Hot coals don't spare the foot of someone who thinks they're different. Neither does adultery spare the one who believes they can manage it, contain it, hide it. The physical world teaches us what the spiritual world knows.

So is he who goes to his neighbor's wife. The parallel is complete and terrible. This isn't a hidden sin; it will find him out. Whoever touches her will not go unpunished. The Lord sees. He cares more than we know.
Men don't despise a thief who steals for hunger. There's mercy here—hunger is a need, and stealing to eat is different from stealing for greed. Even in this, the wise eye sees circumstances.

But if caught, he must restore sevenfold—he gives all the wealth of his house. This is the cost of being caught in theft. And yet notice: there is a price, a path of restitution. Grace doesn't erase law; it works within it.

He who commits adultery is void of understanding. Not of strength or temptation, but of *understanding*—he doesn't see what he's doing to himself. He destroys his own soul. How blind we become when desire leads.

Wounds and dishonor follow. His reproach won't be wiped away. Not forever, but not soon either. Some choices leave marks that become part of our story. The Lord can restore, but restoration takes time.
The jealousy of the husband—rage, fury—isn't petty but righteous. He's been betrayed in his deepest trust. On the day of vengeance, he won't spare. Human justice follows human wrong.
He won't be satisfied by ransom or gifts, no matter how many you offer. Some things can't be bought back. Some roads, once walked, can't be walked out of. This is the Lord's warning, spoken in love.

A father's first word in this long warning: keep my words. Not debate them, not adjust them to suit the moment. Keep them like you keep something precious—held close, guarded. This is love: the gift of a clear path.

Guard my teaching as the apple of your eye—the thing you protect instinctively, without hesitation. Keep my commandments, and the reward is life itself. Not a reward added after, but the very structure of living well.

Bind them on your fingers is the custom of a faithful Jew—the phylactery, worn visible. Write them on the tablet of your heart means carry them deeper, where no one sees but God sees. Both forms matter: the visible commitment and the hidden devotion.

Call wisdom your sister, understanding your relative. Fold them into your family, your closest bonds. When temptation comes—and it will—these faithful companions will be closer to your heart than the stranger's voice.

The strange woman, the foreigner—not always literal. This is anyone who calls you away from faithfulness with words that flatter, that say you deserve more, you're special, rules don't apply to you. Wisdom and understanding keep you from that lie.

A father looks out his window through the lattice—not hidden, but also not exposed. He sees the street, the corner, the people passing. This is pastoral care: watching, knowing what happens in the community you shepherd.

The simple one, void of understanding—young, trusting, not yet tested. He doesn't know himself yet, has no compass. This is why we warn: because youth is the time when one direction looks exactly like another.
Passing through the street near her corner, going the way to her house. Casual steps, small choices. No one wakes one morning planning to be ruined. It's a series of corners, one street at a time.

In the twilight, the evening, the middle of the night—he doesn't notice when he chose the dark. Temptation often arrives cloaked in shadow, in the time when judgment sleeps. The darkness itself is part of the trap.
She met him dressed like a prostitute, with crafty intent. Not accident—intention. She knows exactly what she's doing, and she's chosen him. The predator appears at the moment of his weakness.

Loud and defiant, her feet don't stay in her house—a woman untethered from shame, from the bonds that hold a household together. She's broken free from restraint, and now she uses that freedom as a weapon.

Now in the streets, now in the squares, lurking at every corner. She's everywhere the young man might go. There's no escape because she fills the whole landscape. This is how sin hunts: it's not one door, it's a maze.

She caught him and kissed him with an impudent face. No apology, no pretense of innocence. She acts as though she has every right to him. Boldness is part of her seduction—she makes him feel he's wanted.

Sacrifices of peace offerings, vows paid—she cloaks her offer in religious language. I've fulfilled my duty to God, now I'm celebrating. She makes sin sound like righteousness, makes desire sound like piety. The misuse of faith's own words is one of the deepest lies.

I came out to meet you, I've been seeking your face. She makes him feel chosen, special, pursued. This is the seduction beneath the seduction—she tells him he matters, she chose him. In that moment, he forgets that her hunger is not love.

She describes her bed with carpets and striped Egyptian cloth—luxury, expense, care. She's showing him what she's prepared, what's waiting. The offer isn't just her body; it's comfort, abundance, a world that seems to have no cost.

Myrrh, aloes, cinnamon—expensive perfumes. Every sense is being appealed to, softened, prepared to surrender. The trap is made luxurious so he won't notice it's a trap. Comfort can be as dangerous as pain when it leads you away from God.

Take our fill of loving until morning, solace ourselves with loving. She speaks as though there's time, as though the morning will never come, as though consequences don't exist. She offers him a moment where nothing else matters. That moment is the hook.

My husband isn't home, gone on a long journey. She removes the last barrier—no one to catch them, no one watching. In her story, there's no authority, no law, no one but the two of them. She erases everything outside this room.
He took money, will return at the full moon—she's thought this through. She knows when he'll be back, how much time they have. The detail shows her calculating mind. She's hunted before.

With persuasive words she led him astray, with flattering lips she seduced him. She used his own hunger against him, his own desire to be wanted. He was not forced; he was charmed. That's what makes it so dangerous—he walked willingly into the trap.

Like an ox to the slaughter, like a fool stepping into a noose—he doesn't know what's about to happen. He follows immediately, without hesitation or thought. The warning isn't being heard because his ears are full of her promises.

Until an arrow strikes his liver—a sudden, mortal wound. Like a bird caught unaware, he doesn't see the cost until it's too late. The trap springs shut, and only then does he understand the price of what he wanted.

Now therefore, sons, listen to me. After telling the whole story, the father returns to the young man reading this. Listen: the warning isn't meant to scare you away from life, but to wake you to what's real. Don't learn only from your own ruin.
Don't let your heart turn to her ways, don't go astray in her paths. The battle is won in the heart first, before the feet ever move. Guard your desires, name the lie before it becomes a choice.

She has thrown down many wounded; all her slain are a mighty army. She's not new to this. How many have already fallen? How many families broken, how many futures cut short? This is what unfaithfulness leaves behind: a graveyard.

Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the rooms of death. Readers today hear an echo: every path away from wisdom leads downward. The names change—ambition without conscience, comfort without faithfulness, desire without restraint—but they all lead the same direction. Only the upward way leads home.

Notice wisdom is not silent or hiding. She calls out—actively, boldly. When I was young and thought wisdom was something dusty you found in books, I missed this: she's hunting for us, speaking loud enough to hear.

High places by the road where paths meet—real places travelers saw each other, made decisions. Wisdom plants herself where life happens, where choices meet. She doesn't hide in study halls; she stands where we actually live.
City gates and entry doors—the public space. She isn't whispering secrets for the privileged few. Wisdom cries aloud so the poor, the stranger, the overlooked can hear just as clearly as anyone else.
Not just to the learned or the mighty, but to all mankind—every man, every son of Adam. I've learned that God's wisdom speaks to the farmhand as much as the king. The call is truly for everyone.
She calls the simple to understand prudence. There's kindness in this—no shame, no mockery. She's saying: you can learn, you can grow into wisdom. The door is open right now.

Excellent things, right things. When wisdom speaks, what comes out doesn't aim for entertainment or flattery—it aims for what's true and what's best. I've noticed: the wisest words I've heard were rarely the loudest.
My mouth speaks truth. Wickedness is an abomination to me. After all these years, I see: real wisdom has standards. She isn't flexible about the truth just to please. That's why we can trust her.

Nothing crooked or perverse. Wisdom's words are straight, direct, clean. When I've been confused by someone's speech—when something felt 'off'—it was usually because the path wasn't straight. Honest wisdom feels like relief.

Plain to those who understand, right to those who find knowledge. The wise can see the worth in her words immediately. But you have to be listening, watching for it. Wisdom doesn't hide from the seeker.

Receive my instruction rather than silver, knowledge rather than choice gold. I've watched people choose quick money over learning, and I've watched them regret it. Wisdom's voice says: your growth is worth more than any purchase.

Wisdom better than rubies—in that culture, rubies were wealth's crown jewel, the rarest and most precious treasure. The writer is saying: if you had to choose between a king's ransom in gems or wisdom, choose wisdom. Nothing compares.
I have made prudence my dwelling. Wisdom doesn't just visit; she lives somewhere deep. When I have been truly wise, it's because I made the habit of careful thought my home, not just a guest.
The fear of the Lord is to hate evil. I hate pride, arrogance, evil ways, perverse speech. Wisdom isn't colorless—she has strong loves and strong hates. She despises what destroys people.

Counsel and sound knowledge are mine. Understanding and power—the real kind, not the kind that bullies. I've seen folks with power but no wisdom destroy everything they touch. Real power lives in wisdom.

By me kings reign. This is a breathtaking claim: wisdom is the foundation, not the crown. The mightiest rulers of that world—those who could command armies—are only truly ruling when they rule by her counsel.
Princes rule by me. Noble and righteous rulers—all of them lean on wisdom for their authority. No leader can be just without her. It's a humbling word for anyone who holds power.

I love those who love me. Those who seek me diligently will find me. She's not hidden, not playing hard to get. There's an openness here—almost a tender reaching back toward us. Love for love, seek and find.

Riches, honor, enduring wealth, prosperity. I used to read this as mere promise of stuff. Now I see: when you walk with wisdom, you gain what actually lasts—not the trinkets we panic over, but real substance.
My fruit is better than gold, my yield than choice silver. Wisdom produces a harvest. Unlike gold, which just sits there, wisdom's fruits keep giving, keep nourishing. That's why she's worth more.

I walk in the way of righteousness, in the middle of the paths of justice. She doesn't veer left or right. There's a middle way—not weakness, not harshness, but the actual path that's right. And she walks it faithfully.

That I may give wealth to those who love me. I fill their treasuries. There's real generosity in wisdom. She isn't stingy. Those who pursue her find abundance—not always the kind they expected, but abundance nonetheless.

Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. This shifts the whole tone—we're moving from wisdom as a counselor to wisdom as something eternal, part of God's very nature and work. She's not new. She's ancient.

Set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. I sit with this verse and feel how small my worries are. Wisdom was before mountains, before me, before my greatest fears. She holds a longer story.

When there were no depths, I was born. When there were no springs abounding with water—the ancient waters of chaos itself. Wisdom was present before the world took shape. She wasn't born into uncertainty; she stands above it.

Before the mountains were settled, before the hills, I was born. Mountains were the most solid, immovable thing ancient people knew. And wisdom? She was before them. Nothing in creation is older or more fundamental than her.

Before he made the earth, the fields, the beginning of the dust of the world—all the foundational matter. Wisdom predates creation itself. When I read this, I realize: I'm leaning on something that holds up all things.

When he established the heavens, I was there; when he set a circle on the surface of the deep. She's there at the moment of creation—the horizon, the boundary, the order emerging from chaos. Part of God's creative act itself.

When he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong. Every detail of creation—the weather, the waters—all made through wisdom, with wisdom present. She's woven into how the world holds together.

When he gave the sea its boundary, when he marked the foundations of the earth—limits, order, structure. Wisdom creates boundaries so things don't dissolve into chaos. She's the architect's principle, the order that lets things be.

Then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him. Wisdom is God's companion at creation—a joy, a delight. She doesn't grudge her work; she rejoices in it. There's play in creation.

Rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men. Wisdom delights in what God made, and especially in us—mankind. Imagine: the principle that holds creation together finds joy in human beings. That's a radical kind of love.

Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways. After all that cosmic grandeur—creation, eternity—she turns to us personally. 'My sons.' Not distant, not cold. She calls us hers, and the way to blessing is simply: listen and follow.

Hear instruction, and be wise. Don't refuse it. After all her witness—her words, her power, her joy—there's an urgent, tender plea: hear her. Don't turn away. Don't harden your heart to what she's offering.

Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts. Imagine someone who comes every day, stands at wisdom's door, waiting and watching. That's not casual. That's devoted. And blessing meets that devotion.

For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh. Life itself—not just years, but true life, real living. Finding wisdom is finding life. And more: it opens favor with God. She's the door to everything that matters.

But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul. All those who hate me love death. Readers today hear an echo here that may not have been as clear in ancient times: rejecting wisdom's voice—the wisdom that is Christ—means choosing spiritual death. And yet she still calls, still waits at the gate.

Wisdom builds steadily, with purpose—each pillar set firm. She's not rushing to be noticed. There's beauty in how the Lord establishes understanding in us, stone by stone, the foundation strong enough to bear the weight of a whole life.

All is prepared—the table is ready, not half-done or locked away. This tells me the Father's invitation to learn from Him is never hurried, never stingy. He's already made the feast. We just need to come.

In an ancient city, the highest places were where voices carried—the public plaza where everyone could hear. Wisdom doesn't hide; she calls out plainly. The Spirit of Christ does the same: He speaks where we all can hear, if we'll listen.

"Simple" here doesn't mean foolish—it means unformed, like clay in the potter's hand, not yet shaped by understanding. The Lord loves to welcome the honest beginner, the one who knows they don't know. That's where learning truly starts.

"Come, eat"—the language of hospitality and joy, not duty. Wisdom invites us to taste and know goodness, not to swallow bitter pills. When we draw near to learn, we're called to something nourishing, something that strengthens us from the inside out.

Leaving simple ways is an act of faith—choosing the way you can't yet fully see because you trust the One calling you. Jesus asked His followers to leave behind what they knew. The reward is life that finally makes sense.

Sometimes a word spoken in love bounces off a hardened heart and comes back as anger. This isn't a reason to stop speaking truth—but it's a reason to be wise about whom you're trying to reach. Discernment matters as much as courage.

A wise person hears correction and grows grateful. A foolish one hears it and grows resentful. The difference isn't in the words spoken—it's in the heart that receives them. Jesus said, "Blessed are those who hunger for righteousness." That hunger changes everything.

The wise keep growing. They're not finished, not satisfied with what they know. This restlessness—to understand more, to be wiser, to know God better—is a mark of spiritual health. A stagnant mind is a closed one.

"Fear of Yahweh"—reverence born from knowing who God truly is. To know the Holy One is to stand amazed, humbled, drawn to worship. This awe, this trembling respect for His holiness, is where all real understanding begins. Everything else flows from this.

Wisdom doesn't just help us live longer—it helps us live well. The days multiply, yes, but filled with what? Understanding, peace, fruitfulness, the favor of knowing we're walking with the Lord. A long life without wisdom would be exhausting.

Your choices are your own—wisdom builds you up, mockery tears you down, and you'll carry the weight either way. The Lord doesn't force us to grow. But He does show us the difference between a path that leads upward and one that leads down.

The foolish woman here is not a person—she's a picture of folly itself, loud and uncontrolled. She calls just as loudly as Wisdom does. The tragedy is that many hear her first because she's louder, easier, more fun. But she's also empty inside.

She takes her seat where Wisdom also sits—the high places, the busy city—as if she belonged there. Deception often wears respectability. It sits in the same street corner as truth and shouts just as loud. We must learn to tell the difference.

She calls to those who are already on their way somewhere else, trying to lure them off the path. Temptation often works this way—not pulling you toward something better, but distracting you from where you're meant to go. Stay fixed on your direction.

She uses Wisdom's very words—"simple ones, come here"—but what she's offering is ruin dressed as freedom. This is why knowing God's true voice matters so deeply. The wolf doesn't announce himself; he borrows the shepherd's call.

What tastes sweet to a hungry heart—and so many of us are spiritually hungry—can be the very thing that destroys us. Forbidden fruit, secret pleasures, easy shortcuts all seem delicious until they're consumed. But then? We're left with ashes.

Readers today hear an echo in this warning: we often don't see the true end of the paths we choose until we've walked them far. The dead in Sheol didn't wake up one morning deciding they'd chosen death—they simply never saw it coming. Wisdom calls us to see ahead.

I've seen how the way a child turns out shapes a parent's whole heart. When they walk toward wisdom, something in us finds peace—not because we did it all perfectly, but because we see them reaching toward the Lord.
We all know people who got rich the wrong way. It never stays—the Lord has a way of stripping it all back. But righteousness? That holds up under any weight.
I have watched good people go through thin times, and still He made sure they had what they needed. The wicked may crave, but the Lord sees to His own.
Lazy hands lead to empty pockets—that's just how the world works. But faithful work, even small and steady work, builds something real. The Lord honors hands that move.

Summer is the time of plenty—grain ready, fruit ripe. The wise one sees the season and gathers now, while the sleeper misses it. In Jesus' teaching too, He warns us: the fields are ready, but time moves on. Pay attention when opportunity stands in front of you.
Goodness leaves a mark on the face—blessing shows, even in hard times. The mouth of the wicked, though, grows bitter, covered by the violence they've spoken into the world.
When a good person passes, people remember their name with warmth. But wickedness has a short memory—it rots away. I've seen this. The faithful are remembered; the crooked are forgotten.
The wise heart takes a correction like a gift. The fool, though, can't hold his tongue and chatter chatter chatter—until he stumbles and falls. Silence sometimes is the bravest thing.
A blameless walk gives you solid ground beneath your feet. The crooked path looks clever until the day you're found out, and then everything crumbles. Integrity is simpler—and safer.

A wink, a knowing glance, a hidden signal—those little deceits work their poison. The chatterbox, same as verse 8, can't hold back and falls for it. Small betrayals wear down trust like water on stone.

A spring of living water—that's how Jesus talks to the woman at the well. The righteous person's words are like that: they refresh, they sustain, they give life. The wicked's mouth only covers others in harm.
Hatred is a spark that sets everything burning. But love? Love moves quietly over the wrongs like snow covering the ground. This is the heart of it all—which one will we feed?
Wisdom shows itself in what we say—a discerning person's lips hold understanding. The foolish? They earn the rod, the consequence their own words bring. What you speak shapes what you become.
The wise save things up—knowledge, insight, experience. They grow richer inwardly. The fool's mouth is always running, and it leads him straight to ruin. Quiet gathering beats loud emptying.

Wealth is a fortress for the rich—it shields and protects. But poverty can become a wall too, trapping the poor. This isn't pretty truth, but it's honest. The Lord cares deeply for those with the fewest shields.
Right work leads onward, always a step closer to life with the Lord. Wrong work? It compounds, it multiplies, it breeds more sin. What we do today grows into what we become tomorrow.
The one who takes correction is on the way of life—the Lord is still reaching him. But the one who shrugs off rebuke? He leads others astray too. Our choices ripple outward.
To hide hatred behind sweet words is to fill your mouth with lies. And slander? That's when the lie becomes loud. The Lord sees both the silence and the speech.

Many words mean many chances to slip into disobedience—to boast, to deceive, to hurt. But the restrained tongue? There's wisdom in that. I've learned that the best thing I said was often the thing I didn't say.

Choice silver—precious, rare, refined by fire. That's what the righteous tongue is like. The wicked's heart, meanwhile, is worth little, producing little of value. In Scripture, silver often speaks of redemption; the righteous tongue points toward Christ.
The righteous feed others—with words, with care, with truth spoken at the right time. The foolish starve, not because no one offers bread, but because they never learned to listen.
The Lord's blessing brings wealth—not strain, not sleepless worry. When the Lord gives, it settles like morning dew. Much of our toil is sorrow because we chase it without Him.
A fool gets a thrill from doing wrong—for now. But the understanding person? His pleasure is deeper, rooted in what lasts. What makes you laugh says something about what you love.

The wicked fear something, and it comes to pass—like they've called it down on themselves. The righteous, though, have desires that the Lord grants. Fear shapes what comes; faith opens what's hoped for.

When the storm tears through, the wicked are scattered like leaves. But the righteous? They stand. Not unmoved, perhaps, but rooted. I've seen this in times of trial—who stands and who falls tells you who was built on rock.

Vinegar on teeth—a shudder of sourness. Smoke in the eyes—tears and blindness. The sluggard is that kind of irritant to everyone around him. It's a picture drawn from life, the way a lazy person's habit wears on those who depend on him.
To fear the Lord is to add days to your life—not just years, but a kind of fullness. The wicked shorten theirs by the very striving that consumes them. One path lengthens; one eats itself.

The righteous look forward to something that will not fail. Their hope has a ground. The wicked's hope, though, is built on sand. When you want something the Lord doesn't will, that hope simply perishes.

The way of the Lord is a fortress—safe, strong, a place to stand. But to the worker of iniquity, it's a wall, a trap, a ruin. The very thing that saves one destroys another, depending on which side you're on.
The righteous are planted—they remain. The wicked, no matter how firm they seem, will not dwell in the land. The Lord is patient, but He is not careless. Justice moves quietly until it arrives.
A righteous mouth brings forth wisdom—the overflow of a wise heart. The perverse tongue? It is cut off. We make ourselves by what we speak; our words are the soil of our own becoming.

The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable—they've learned, over time, what brings life. Readers today hear an echo in this: the Spirit teaches us too what to say and when. Looking back, I see how often the Lord quieted me just before I would have spoken harm, or opened my mouth when a word was needed. We're not left to guess.

False weights were the marketplace cheat of ancient days—a merchant's quiet theft. But the Lord sees the heart that wants to be honest before the scales. He takes delight in the straight deal, the kept promise, the person who won't gain a shekel by a lie.

Pride always tumbles into shame because it blinds us to truth. But humility—the willingness to be small—clears our eyes. That's where real wisdom begins: not in what we think we know, but in the room we make for what we don't.

I've watched upright people stumble in darkness, and their integrity was like a compass still pointing home. For the treacherous, it's the opposite—their own twisted dealings become a snare they lay for themselves, and they trip on it.

In the day of judgment, no bank account will buy your peace. But righteousness—the steady habit of walking with God and treating others well—that alone can deliver you from death's grip. This is the only currency that lasts.

The blameless don't stumble because their way is made straight by who they are. But wickedness carries its own weight—each wrong turn makes the next one steeper, until at last the wicked fall by the very hand they've made themselves.

Righteousness is a rescue rope. The unfaithful, meanwhile, are so tangled in their own desires that they become their own captors. What begins as a want becomes a need; what began as freedom becomes a chain.
When a wicked person dies, their schemes die with them—all the power they grasped for scatters like dust. There's a loneliness to a life built on wickedness; nothing of it outlasts the grave.
The righteous slip out of the very trap the wicked walks into. It's not luck—it's that goodness itself is a different kind of road. The wicked travels his own path and finds its destination.

A godless mouth wounds—careless words, rumors, flattery meant to scheme. But the righteous are delivered by knowing what is true: the truth about God, the truth about themselves, the truth about their neighbor. Knowledge is both shield and sword.

When good people prosper, the whole city breathes easier—their blessing spreads like light. When the wicked fall, there is relief, a glad shout. Even cities know the difference between righteousness and ruin.

The blessings of upright people—their prayers, their example, their steady goodness—lift an entire city. But one wicked voice, amplified and believed, can tear down walls that took generations to build.

To despise a neighbor is a poverty of spirit; you've written yourself out of God's own family. A person of understanding knows better—they hold their tongue and hold their heart open instead, even to those they don't understand.

Gossip is betrayal dressed as conversation. It feels like power in the moment, but it costs you trust—the only currency that truly matters. A person of trustworthy spirit guards what was told to them in confidence as if it were gold.
A nation without wise counsel stumbles in the dark and falls. But many counselors? They see what one person alone never could. Wisdom loves company and grows sharper when it's tested by other minds.

In ancient commerce, to pledge yourself as surety for a stranger was a serious and costly risk. Solomon warns: this kind of binding oath will bring you sorrow. Wisdom is knowing where to draw the line between generosity and self-harm.

A gracious woman wins honor the quiet way: by how she speaks, how she listens, how she lifts others. Violent men may grab riches through force, but she gathers something deeper—the respect of those who know her heart.

Mercy is not weakness; it's a gift you give yourself. When you show kindness, your own soul flourishes. But cruelty festers in the one who practices it—it troubles the very flesh of the cruel person, eats away at them from inside.

Wicked wages are hollow—they come and go like smoke. But righteousness is a seed that bears real fruit; what you sow in God's field comes back true and lasting. One crop is illusion; the other is harvest.

Here the choice is laid bare as simply as it can be. Righteousness leads to life; evil pursuits lead to death. Not in the next world only, but here—in the kind of life you're actually living, the freedom or bondage you taste each day.

The twisted heart is an abomination to the Lord because He sees it—He knows the knots of deception, the turns meant to hide the self from Him. But those whose ways are blameless? He looks on them with delight, the way a gardener admires an unblemished rose.

Evil never escapes entirely; it collects like debt. But the righteous carry something forward—their children inherit not just genes but a legacy, a shelter built on faithfulness. The blessing follows them.

A gold ring adorns a pig's snout—a striking image of waste and mismatch. So too a beautiful woman who lacks discernment: her loveliness cannot hide the recklessness, the poor judgment. Beauty without wisdom becomes its own kind of ugliness.

The righteous person's desire is for good—true good, not the glittering counterfeit. And what they expect, they are not disappointed in. The wicked, meanwhile, braces for wrath; his own expectation is his companion misery.

A generous scattering—a widow's coins, a parent's time, a meal shared—somehow multiplies. But hoarding, the tight grip? It turns to dust. There's a paradox in God's economy: open hands gain wealth; closed hands lose even what they hold.
A liberal soul grows fat—nourished by its own giving. And those who water others' fields find their own well overflowing. This is how grace works: what flows from you returns to you, multiplied.

In grain-dependent cultures, withholding grain in famine is a grave sin—the community curses such a hoarder. But he who sells at fair price? Blessing crowns his head. Even in hardship, fair dealing summons God's favor.
Seek good with diligence, and favor finds you—doors open, grace appears. But hunt for evil, and evil comes running toward you. We tend to find what we look for; the seeker shapes the search.
A man who trusts in riches has built his house on sand; when the wind blows, it falls. But the righteous, rooted in God, flourish like the green leaf—alive, supple, growing even in lean times.

Troubles your own house through wickedness or folly, and you inherit the wind—nothing solid, all emptiness. The foolish become servants to the wise not by force but by the natural weight of their choices. Wisdom builds; folly dismantles.

The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life—shade and sustenance for others, roots that hold the soil. And a wise heart wins souls not through argument but through quiet faithfulness, drawing others toward the life they see lived out.

Readers today hear an echo in this verse: if the righteous barely escape, scarcely receive their reward—how much more will the wicked and sinful face justice? The asymmetry is striking. We live in a world where God takes righteousness seriously enough to require its fruit to be earned, not given. As of 2026-10, this reminds us that grace is not cheap, nor is judgment arbitrary.

I've watched people divide into two kinds: those who welcome a hard word because they hunger to grow, and those whose pride makes them brittle against any mirror. The first kind walk closer to Jesus; they know He loves them too much to let them stay small.
Favor is not mere luck—it falls on the heart that means well. Yahweh's gaze rests on the honest soul, and His opposition finds the schemer. I've learned to trust that what looks hidden is known.

Evil is a house built on sand. I've watched wicked plans collapse under their own weight while the righteous—with shallow roots that seem frail—endure. There's a stability in doing right that no scheme can shake.

A wife of worth is her husband's ornament, his pride, the thing that makes him want to be better. A woman of shame eats him from inside like rot. One calls forth his best; the other drags him down into ruin.

The righteous heart thinks straight; it sees to the root of a matter. The wicked person's mind is a crooked path—what they say may glitter, but it's poisoned at its core. I've learned to watch where counsel comes from, not just how it sounds.
The wicked speak in ambushes—their words are traps. But the righteous speak and rescue; their tongue becomes a rope flung into the darkness. In this world of lies, honesty is a form of mercy.

Wickedness burns itself out. I've seen it: the schemes fail, the liars get caught, the proud fall. But the righteous house stands—not because nothing touches it, but because it rests on stone. That's the difference.
A person is known by their wisdom—others see it and give honor where it's due. But a twisted mind earns only scorn. The world may reward cleverness for a season, but it respects wisdom always.

Better to be humble and fed than proud and starving. There's a kind of person who'd rather go hungry than be seen doing work, and another who gladly serves—and the second one sleeps well. Pride is expensive; humility pays.

The righteous one cares for his beast—feeds it, tends it, sees its need as his charge. That small kindness is a window into his soul: a man who rules his own house will treat even the creatures under his hand with gentleness. The wicked, by contrast, are cruel even where cruelty gains nothing; it reveals a hardness at their center.
The farmer who works his plot has bread. The dreamer who chases foolish schemes has nothing but air. I've seen it plainly: steady work feeds; idle fantasy starves. The Lord rewards the diligent hand.

The wicked crave the spoils of wickedness—they want what evil can steal. But the righteous are rooted in their own soil, and from that root something good grows. One seeks from the outside; the other grows from within.
The man caught in his own lies is trapped—his words become his prison. But the righteous person, even in deep trouble, finds a way through. There's a freedom in truth that lies can never grant.

Your words feed you—good words bring good return. Your labor is not lost; what your hands build comes back to you. It's not magic; it's how the Lord has woven the world together. Care shapes what you harvest.
A fool trusts his own judgment completely—he is always right in his own mind. But the wise person listens, considers, and learns from others. Humility is the door to wisdom; certainty is its lock.

A fool wears his anger on his face, shows his annoyance before sunset—he's mastered nothing. The wise person, slighted or insulted, keeps his peace; he knows his own worth doesn't depend on what others say. That's the quiet strength of self-knowledge.

The truthful witness speaks what he saw and knows. The false witness makes up what serves him. One builds a world you can trust; the other poisons everything. In a community of truth-tellers, you can breathe.

There are words that cut like a sword—harsh, careless, meant to wound. But the wise tongue is like a physician's touch, tending what hurts. I've learned to listen for which kind a person speaks, and to speak healing when I can. That's how Jesus teaches us to use our mouths.

The truth spoken today is truth tomorrow and the day after—it has legs. A lie is quick but dies fast; it can't keep its footing. I've noticed that liars must work harder and harder to cover the first lie, while the truthful person rests.

The person plotting harm carries that weight inside—their heart is a nest of deceit. But those who work for peace carry something light and clean. I've seen it in their faces: one looks like a prisoner, the other like someone coming home.

Trouble touches everyone, but the righteous are never overcome by it—something in them won't break. The wicked, meanwhile, pile evil upon evil, and that pile becomes their grave. The Lord protects His own.

Yahweh hates lying lips—not the person, but the lie itself. He delights in those who do the truth. There's a simplicity here that I've come to treasure: the Lord's gaze is fixed on whether you're living truly, and He takes delight in honesty like a father beams at his child.

The prudent person holds their knowledge close—not from pride, but from wisdom; they know when to speak and when to listen. The fool's heart is an open mouth broadcasting his foolishness. Silence is not weakness; sometimes it's the deepest skill.

The diligent hand rises to lead; effort earns authority. The lazy hand finds itself serving—bound, trapped, no longer free to choose. I've watched it: discipline opens doors; laziness closes them one by one.

Worry is a weight that presses down—a man's heart grows heavy with it. But a kind word—just one—can lift that load right off. I've been both that anxious heart and the person who spoke the small kindness, and I know which is the greater gift.

The righteous person is careful in friendship—he knows who to trust, where to walk. The wicked person is led astray by his own desires, following each impulse off the cliff. One thinks before he follows; the other is led by blind appetite.

The lazy hunter doesn't even cook his kill—he can't be bothered. But the diligent person guards what he has, tends it, and it multiplies. The difference isn't luck; it's care. One man's carelessness is another man's treasure.

The path of righteousness leads to life; there is no death on that way—at least not the death that matters. Readers today hear an echo in this: Jesus has walked that way ahead of us, and He calls us to follow. To walk with Him is to walk away from death and toward the only life that never ends.
How quickly we learn that listening to wisdom—really listening—sets us on better ground. The scoffer thinks he knows better; but the wise child knows his father has walked longer roads.
Words are so much more powerful than we give them credit. A man who speaks wisely finds himself surrounded by good things—not by luck, but by the simple law that good words open good doors.
The mouth is the gate to the soul. I've watched this: those who hold their tongue in hard moments protect something sacred inside. Restraint is often the bravest thing.
Desire without work is only a dream that makes the heart heavier. But the one who works, even when it's hard—their hunger becomes fuel, and the satisfaction runs deep.
There's a clear line drawn here: the righteous person is built differently. Truth matters to them, not because it pays but because who you are depends on it.
Integrity is like a shield you don't even know you're wearing—until the day you need it. Righteousness tends you. Wickedness? It catches up with itself.
How we judge by appearances and get it backwards every time. Some pretend to have, some pretend to lack. Real wealth and real poverty run deeper than anyone's front door.
A sobering word about wealth—it can save your skin when danger comes. But the poor live more freely than they know; they have nothing that can be taken from them.
Light and lamp—the righteous carry something that keeps burning. The wicked carry only what will go dark. I've seen it: a good life has a warmth that shows.
Pride opens its mouth and finds quarrels waiting. But the humble person—the one who listens—walks into wisdom the way you walk into a room where people actually care.
Quick money won dishonestly doesn't stay. It's restless. But what you build slowly, honestly, with your own hands grows and takes root because it's real.
I know this verse in my bones: waiting wears on you. But when what you've hoped for finally comes, it's more than relief—it's life returning. The Lord knows how long we can bear to wait.
Instruction is a gift, not an insult. The fool thinks it's an attack; the wise know it's a hand offered. And the one who grasps it finds himself rewarded—not by accident, but by the shape of things.
Wise teaching is running water—it quenches and gives life. It turns us away from the snares we can't see coming. The wise know this and drink deep.
A humble understanding—really seeing how things work—wins people over. Not by flattery, but because truth is attractive. The unfaithful life, though, is always climbing uphill.
The wise person thinks before they act. They know things. The fool? He just opens his mouth and proves he knows nothing at all.
Trust is a fragile thing to carry. A faithless messenger breaks under the weight and falls. But one who keeps faith—they bring healing just by showing up.

The refusal to learn costs everything—poverty, shame, a diminished name. But the one who hears correction, who's willing to change? He walks toward honor because he's willing to become who he should be.
When longing finds its answer, the soul tastes something sweet—real and deep. But the fool? He'll turn away from what's good rather than turn from his own way.
You become like the company you keep—I've seen it plainly. Walk with wise ones, and you grow. Keep fools' company, and something inside you slowly diminishes.
Sin doesn't let you go easily—trouble finds its way to you. But righteousness? It opens doors. Not by magic, but because goodness shapes the ground you walk on.

A good legacy goes to the third generation—the children's children. What you build with integrity lasts. But the wicked? What they gather ends up in righteous hands because the Lord knows whose it should be.
Here's the cruel paradox: the poor work hard and grow food from thin soil. But injustice sweeps it all away. This verse calls for justice, not resignation.
Hard words about discipline. But look: to spare is to hate; to discipline with care is to love. The parent who loves will sometimes say no when it costs them something.

Readers today hear an echo: the righteous eat to the filling of the soul. There's a satisfaction that isn't just full—it's contentment. Meanwhile the wicked go hungry no matter what's on the table. We taste the difference.

A woman's hands can build—or tear. I've watched homes held together by quiet choices, day after day, while others crumble under the weight of haste and carelessness. The Lord sees both kinds of strength.
Uprightness isn't perfection—it's a stubborn love of the Lord that shapes your path. When you fear Him truly, your feet know where they're going, even in dim light.

The 'rod to his back'—in ancient judgment, the fool's own careless words invited correction, sometimes public shame. The wise know that what leaves your lips lives on in other hearts; better to think before you speak.
A hard saying—clean hands come easy if you risk nothing, but the work of increase is costly. The Lord often chooses the path that builds real fruit over the path that keeps life tidy and small.
Truth settles in the belly of a faithful witness like ballast. A false witness? Their lies spring up like weeds, choking everything they touch. The Lord knows which kind you are.

A scoffer hunts for wisdom but won't recognize it when he finds it—his pride stands in the way. But the discerning? They see knowledge the way a child sees bread at the table. Open hands receive easily.
