Some company will hollow you out. There's a kindness in stepping back from a fool—not in pride, but in protecting what little wisdom the Lord has given you. Not every voice deserves your ear.
The prudent person pauses and thinks through the way ahead. The fool? He mistakes his own cunning for wisdom, then wonders why doors close. One is built on truth; the other on sand.

Atonement—the great covering that ancient Israel knew. Fools mock what they don't understand; the upright recognize that broken things need mending. In Christ, we see the fullness of what 'good will' truly means.
Your deepest joy and deepest sorrow—no stranger can really live there with you. Only the Lord knows the width and depth of what you carry. That loneliness is also a threshold to His presence.
The house built on wickedness trembles, even before the wind. The tent of the upright—pitched on nothing but the Lord's faithfulness—holds. Which foundation would you rather stand on?
This verse haunts me—how many paths seemed right to me until the Lord gently turned me around? Beware the road that flatters you. Truth often looks harder at first.
Laughter can wear a mask. I've learned that the loudest joy in a room sometimes hides the deepest wound. The Lord sees beneath the smile to the true state of the heart.
Each person tastes what their own ways produce. Plant unfaithfulness and you harvest emptiness; plant faithfulness and you find that the Lord's hand is not idle. He rewards, but in His time.
The simple believe everything because they haven't learned suspicion yet—not all innocence is wisdom. The prudent person pauses, thinks, checks the way. That pause is where grace often whispers.

Fear of the Lord is not timidity—it's a wise recoil from evil, the way a child instinctively pulls back from fire. The fool charges ahead thinking himself invulnerable. One choice leads to life, the other to ash.
Quick anger and craftiness are cousins—both are ways of not waiting, not yielding. The Lord's way is patience. A hasty tongue makes enemies; a careful heart makes room for wisdom.
The simple inherit what they were taught without question; the prudent reach out and take hold of knowledge. One is passive, the other active. Which will you be?
In the end, the good stand and the wicked bow. Not always today—but the Lord doesn't measure by a day. His justice is patient, thorough, and sure.
Wealth gathers crowds; poverty gathers silence. This isn't how it should be, and yet it is. But the Lord remembers the poor—He never forgets them the way the world does.
To despise your neighbor is to raise your fist against the very image of your Maker. But to lean toward the poor with kindness? That honors the God who made you both.

Those who plot evil wander into the fog—they don't see the edges of their own schemes. Those who plan good find themselves held by love and faithfulness, as if the Lord Himself were walking beside them.
In ancient economies as now: honest labor—the strength of the ox in the field—yields real increase. Mere talk, however pleasant, produces nothing but hunger. The Lord rewards the work of our hands.
The wise wear their riches lightly—wealth serves them, not the other way around. The fool's crown is folly itself, and it's the heaviest thing he'll ever carry.
A truthful witness can save a life—sometimes literally, sometimes by preserving justice where it would crumble. Your honesty matters more than you know.
In the fear of the Lord, you find a fortress stronger than any wall of stone. Your children inherit that fortress when they see it lived out in your life. That's real wealth.
Fear of the Lord isn't dread—it's the fountain that keeps you alive. Many paths lead to death, but this one? It leads to life, over and over again.
A king surrounded by many counselors stands secure; a prince without followers crumbles. The principle holds for all leadership—we need one another. Isolation is a slow death.
Patience is the mark of a deep mind. The slow-to-anger person has room to think, to feel, to choose. Quick temper? It's foolishness stepping forward to speak.
A peaceful heart is the body's friend; envy is poison that no doctor can cure. You choose which one lives in you. Choose peace, and watch what the Lord does with it.
When you crush the poor, you spit on the God who made them. When you are kind, you honor His image in them. It's that simple. It's that serious.
The wicked find themselves falling with no net beneath them. The righteous? Even in death, they rest in the refuge the Lord has been all along. That's why the righteous fear Him and live.
Wisdom rests quiet in a discerning heart, but it can't hide—it shows itself in what that person does and says. The fool carries his folly on his forehead; you read it the moment he opens his mouth.

Readers today hear an echo in this verse—a nation that walks in righteousness, with justice and mercy woven through its laws, stands tall and endures. But one sunk in sin? Its shame spreads like cracks in a foundation. As of 2026-10, we see this truth play out again and again.
A servant who conducts his work with wisdom wins favor—even a king sees and rewards such faithfulness. But shame? It courts the king's anger swiftly. Your character speaks louder than your station.
I've seen how a soft word can stop an argument before it swells. The heart recognizes kindness, even when we're upset. When we choose gentleness, we're following the One who spoke peace into storms.

The wise person speaks to teach; the fool speaks to spill what's inside. There's a difference between using words to help others understand and using them as a bucket for every thought that comes. Wisdom waits, listens, chooses.

Yahweh's gaze rests on all things—the hidden cruelty and the secret kindness. This isn't meant to frighten us but to draw us home. He sees the good we do when no one applauds, and He sees what we're hiding. Either way, we're known.
A kind word grows life like a tree—slowly, steadily, bearing fruit for years. But deceit poisons even the speaker. When we live by truth, we nourish not just others but our own soul.
The fool hears correction and hardens his heart; the wise one hears it and learns. The door opens or closes based on what we do with an honest word. Pride shuts; humility opens.
In the righteous household there is treasure—not always coins, but stability, peace, and the freedom to do good. The wicked's gain brings only unease. Character is the real wealth that stays.
The wise mouth shares what grows in a wise heart; the fool's heart is a wasteland. We teach what we've learned and what we've become. The lips follow.

Yahweh turns from the wicked's sacrifices—even the grandest ones—because the giver's heart is crooked. But the prayer of one seeking to live rightly delights Him. He values the heart's posture over the gift's price.
Yahweh abhors the path of evil, yet He loves the one who walks in righteousness. This is His character: He opposes the way, not the wanderer beyond redemption. He draws us toward life.
Harsh discipline comes for those who leave the way, and the scoffer who refuses reproof walks into ruin. The voice calling us back is mercy; refusing to listen is refusing life itself.

Sheol and Abaddon—the grave and destruction—lie open before Yahweh's sight. If death itself cannot hide from Him, how much more does He see into human hearts? We cannot escape His knowledge, only hide from it or rest in it.
The scoffer loves his own way too much to be corrected, and he avoids the wise person who would remind him. Pride keeps its own company—lonely, though it doesn't know it.
A happy heart radiates outward; an aching one shadows everything. The face tells the truth the tongue might hide. Joy and sorrow mark us—and mark those around us—more than we know.
The understanding heart hunts for wisdom like a miner for gold; the fool feeds on folly as if it were bread. What we hunger for shapes what we become.

The afflicted person sees only the weight of each day, but a cheerful heart turns each day into a feast—not because circumstances change, but because the heart has changed its eyes. Joy is a choice the spirit can make.
A little held with reverence for Yahweh is worth more than riches seized with trouble. The first brings peace; the second brings sleeplessness. We cannot buy rest with stolen goods.

A simple meal—vegetables grown by hand—shared in love surpasses the finest ox when hatred sits at the table. This speaks to how the culture of a home matters more than its abundance. The presence of love seasons everything.
The angry person is a spark; the patient one is a blanket smothering the fire. Our temperament either fuels conflict or quiets it. We each carry this power in our chest.
The lazy person's way is overgrown, thorned, impassable; the upright walk a cleared path. This isn't cruelty but truth: the path of discipline becomes smooth, while neglect lets the weeds take over.
A wise son brings joy to his father; a foolish man scorns his mother. The love we show those who bore us reflects something deep about who we've chosen to become.

The empty-headed person laughs at folly as if it were play; the one with understanding walks a straight road. Knowing the difference between foolishness and wisdom is itself the beginning of understanding.
Plans crumble when made alone; they stand when many voices counsel. Wisdom listens. Fools decide in their own echo chamber.
A timely word brings deep joy—not the fleeting kind but the kind that settles into a person's bones. Speaking truth at exactly the right moment is a gift of grace.
For the wise, life's path leads upward, away from Sheol's descent. This is the promise: choose wisdom, and you choose life, not death. The road goes both directions; we choose which way to walk.

Yahweh will uproot the proud household but preserves the widow's boundaries. His eye is on the vulnerable; the proud cannot stand against Him. This was the ancient truth: the mighty fall, the helpless are kept.
Yahweh detests wickedness even in thought; He delights in a clean mind. He sees not just what we do but what we turn over in the secret dark. Purity begins where no one watches.
The greedy person's grab for more destroys his own home; the one who refuses a bribe keeps his life steady. Corruption eats from the inside out. Integrity is the house's foundation.
The righteous heart weighs its words before speaking; the wicked mouth floods without thinking. The wise person's tongue is governed by a quiet heart; the fool's by an unruly one.
Yahweh is distant from the wicked but bends close to hear the righteous pray. Distance and nearness are not physical but relational—the fruit of the life we've chosen to live.
A bright eye makes the heart glad; good news heals the very bones. These small words—kindness in a glance, truth in a message—carry more healing power than we often know.
The ear that hears reproof learns to live; such a one will dwell at home among the wise. To receive correction is to find your true family—those who see you and love you enough to say hard things.

The person who refuses correction hates their own soul—a hard truth, yet readers today hear an echo in it. Refusing help is refusing life. As I look back at my own long refusals, I see now how much they cost me. But those who listen to reproof find understanding waiting at the end of a humbling road.
The fear of Yahweh is the grammar of wisdom; humility comes before honor. We learn the language of the kingdom by revering its King and bowing low. The ascent always begins on our knees.

We can plan all we like, but the Lord has the final say in how our words land. I've learned that the kindest intention can stumble on a careless phrase, yet grace sometimes speaks through our lips when we weren't even trying. What matters is that we yield our tongue to Him.

We're good at convincing ourselves our motives are pure. I've done it myself—dressed up selfishness in the clothes of virtue. But the Lord sees straight through to what's really driving us. That's both terrifying and oddly liberating, because it means we don't have to hide.

"Commit your deeds to Yahweh"—what a relief to roll the burden off my shoulders and onto His. This is the prayer of the weary and the wise: not bargaining with the Almighty, but handing Him the mess I made and trusting He knows what to do with it.

The Lord made everything—yes, even the wicked and their destruction—toward His own purposes. This doesn't excuse evil, but it does assure me that nothing catches Him off guard. Even rebellion serves His long arc of justice, though we see only a yard of thread.

Pride—that hard, closed heart that thinks it needs no one—stands against everything God is. He can't abide it because it's a wall between Him and us. The proud person loses not just the Lord's favor but the chance to know Him at all.

Mercy covers what we've done; truth keeps us from doing it again. Together they're the path home—the forgiveness that clears the air and the fear of the Lord that steadies our feet. Without both, one is just sentiment and the other just rules.

I've seen enemies soften when a good soul walks past. There's something in right living that disarms even hardened hearts—not through force, but through the Lord's quiet work. It's one of His gentler miracles, and I'm grateful I've lived long enough to witness it.

A little bread eaten with peace and a clear conscience fills the belly better than a banquet stolen or gotten by stepping on others. I've known poor folk who seemed rich in spirit, and rich folk who looked hungry all the time.

I make my plans carefully—the map, the itinerary—and the Lord smiles and says "Watch this." Some of my best days came from the detours He sent. The real wisdom is holding my plans lightly and trusting His redirections more than my own compass.

In ancient courts, the king's word carried the weight of law itself. But even a king is called to speak from a place of wisdom and truth, not mere authority. His lips are to be a conduit of justice, not a weapon of whim.

Honest scales and true weights—the daily tools of commerce in the marketplace—are the Lord's handiwork. He cares about the mundane: whether you cheat your customer by a handful of grain, whether your measure is fair. Integrity in the small things is His concern.

A throne built on wrong is a throne built on sand. The Lord won't shore it up. I've seen powerful men fall because they thought their power was their foundation, when really it was only meant to be a platform for justice. That's what lasts.
Kings love those who speak truth—not flattery, not convenience, but the hard honest word. And so does the Lord. Speaking truth costs courage, but it builds a trust nothing else can.

Fury from someone in power can end a life. But wisdom knows how to turn that anger away—not through fear, but through the kind word that reminds even a wrathful heart of what it's become. There's a bravery in that too.

To be in the good favor of a king or any authority is to be blessed—life flows from approval. How much more, then, to rest under the favor of the Lord, the spring rain that comes after drought? His face toward us is life itself.

I chose poorly when I was young—chased things that glittered. Now I'd trade all of it for the quiet clarity that wisdom brings, the deep knowledge of how to live. Gold you can lose in a night; wisdom stays with you to the grave.

The way of the upright is clear—turn away from evil—and in that clarity is safety. Your soul knows when you're walking the path meant for you, and it knows when you're wandering into the dark. Pay attention to that knowing.

Pride comes before the fall—I've seen it in others and felt it in myself, that moment of air under my feet before the hard ground. Pride is the soil where every downfall is planted. A humble heart, though it kneels, stays standing.

I'd rather sit humbly with those who have little and know it than feast with the proud who believe they got it all themselves. There's more grace in a poor heart than in a rich one with no room in it for God.

The one who listens to the Word and trusts the Lord—that's the blessed one. Not because life becomes easier, but because it becomes secure. You're not adrift; you belong to Someone who knows what He's doing.

The wise heart carries wisdom into speech, and kind words open ears for learning. I've noticed that the people I want to listen to are the ones who don't talk much, but when they do, you feel them thinking of you. That's the fruit of a wise heart.

Understanding is life itself—not the life of the body alone, but the life that knows itself and knows its Maker. Without it, a fool can have everything and be drinking poison the whole time, not knowing why he grows weaker.

The wise person's mouth is a teacher's mouth because the heart is teaching the mouth what to say. What comes out is shaped by years of listening to the Lord and learning His ways. That's not eloquence; that's maturity.

Pleasant words are like honey—they sweeten even a difficult day and heal something deep in the soul. I've felt it myself when someone spoke kindly to me at the right moment. Words matter more than we know.

There is a path that looks right to our eyes, and we take it with confidence, only to find it leads to ruin. This is why we need guides—elders, Scripture, the Spirit—to tell us what our eyes can't see from the ground.

A laborer's hunger is his own motivation—he works because his belly calls. There's an honest simplicity in that: the need drives the effort, and the effort meets the need. It's the way of the world, and it's as it should be.

A worthless man—one with nothing good in his heart to give—devises harm and speaks it like fire that scorches everyone near him. His words are weapons, and his whole aim is destruction. Guard your ears and your company from such a one.

A perverse man stirs up strife, and a whisperer—one who speaks in corners—separates even close friends. This describes the ancient poison of gossip and insinuation, still at work today. One who divides friends is doing the enemy's work.

A violent man is a seducer—he draws others into his harm, making them think they're choosing when really he's leading them astray. Violence corrupts not just the victim but the one who watches and learns to admire it.

When someone winks and compresses their lips—that tiny sign language of conspiracy—they're bent on something wicked. The small gestures often betray the hidden heart. Watch for them in those who seem too careful about how they move.

Gray hair is a crown—not of years alone, but of righteousness. I wear mine as a mark of the Lord's mercy, that He kept me here this long and somehow, by His grace, I didn't waste it. That's the true glory of age.

Self-mastery—ruling your own spirit—is mightier than armies. Any person can swing a sword, but to hold your tongue when it wants to wound, to still your rage when it wants to roar? That takes a strength the world doesn't recognize. The Lord does.

Readers today hear an echo in this verse: we still cast our lots—not dice anymore, but we make choices, spin the wheel, take our chances—and somehow the Lord's hand is in every outcome. Looking back, I see His fingerprints on every decision that seemed random, every path that seemed to choose itself. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful for the sovereignty I didn't always trust.
Peace at the table matters more than plenty. I've learned a quiet home, even with little to eat, holds more blessing than a crowded feast full of sharp words.
The Lord looks at the heart. A servant with good sense does better by Him than a child who refuses wisdom — and He notices.
He tests the hearts. Fire refines metal; Yahweh refines souls — every trial, a brush stroke in His design for us.
Bad company whispers in the ear. Watch what you listen to — your ears shape your soul.
To mock the poor is to mock their Maker. When you look with scorn at those who suffer, you're looking at God's own image — humbled for a time.
Grandchildren's faces, parents' legacy — both are God's gift to us. The long view holds such joy.
Grandiose talk, lies from a leader — both are out of place, like a foreign accent at home. They ring false.
A bribe looks like magic to the giver — opens every door, they think. But it opens the wrong ones.
When you cover a friend's shame with silence, you build love. When you repeat it, you build ruin. Choose quietness.
A wise person learns from a single rebuke; a fool won't change even after a hundred blows. The difference is not in the pain but in the heart's willingness to hear.
Rebellion wages war on itself. The person bent on fighting will find an enemy — sometimes a fierce one.
A mother bear defending her young is less dangerous than a fool defending his own foolishness — there's no reasoning with him.
Evil paid back for good is a poison that doesn't leave the house — it settles in, generation after generation.
Quarrels are like water seeking cracks in a dam. Stop them early, while they're small, or they'll drown everything.
To call a wicked person righteous and a righteous person wicked — both are abomination to Him. Truth matters, even when it costs.
A fool with coins buys everything except sense. No amount of silver can buy what he has no heart to hold.
A true friend loves steadfast; a brother stands in hard seasons. That's not just companionship — that's Christ's own image, showing through.
To pledge yourself for a stranger's debt is recklessness, not kindness. Wisdom keeps some distance, even in generosity.
A love of strife and a grand gate both signal the same thing — pride that builds its own destruction.
A twisted heart and a deceitful tongue — both lead to the same place: trouble that won't let go.
To father a fool cuts you deeply. The parent who watches their child choose foolishness knows a grief all their own.
A joyful heart is medicine. A crushed spirit — that kills from the inside. The invisible thing, the heart's lightness, matters more than the body's strength.
The wicked person takes his bribe in the shadows to twist justice. Corruption loves darkness — it cannot bear the light.
The person of understanding fixes his face toward wisdom, like a compass pointing true. The fool's eyes scatter to every horizon, lost.
A foolish child — how he grieves the father, how he wounds the mother who bore him. Love doesn't heal that wound quickly.
To punish the righteous for doing right is twisted justice — it dishonors the very ones who keep the way true.
A few measured words, a steady temper — readers today hear an echo in a world that shouts. Silence, when chosen with care, speaks with more weight than noise.
Even a fool can seem wise if he keeps his mouth shut. Silence is a mask that hides the heart — but not forever.
I've learned that a heart set on pleasing itself alone grows smaller and harder. The selfish person builds walls instead of bridges, and in the end, finds only the echo of his own voice.
A fool loves the sound of his own thoughts more than the truth itself. He's not really listening—he's just waiting for his turn to speak.
When a person turns away from what's good, shame follows like a shadow. Wickedness is its own harsh teacher.
Like deep waters and flowing brooks—images familiar to those who dwelt by Jordan and desert springs—the wise person's words run deep and give life. The foolish speak only from shallow pools.
God cares deeply about justice. When we favor the powerful over the powerless, we reject the Lord's own heart for the vulnerable.
A fool's mouth is like a match dropped carelessly—it ignites strife wherever he goes. His own words become the rod that strikes him.
I've noticed how often we trap ourselves with our own words. What we speak casually can become the chains that bind us.
Gossip is like bread broken at table—it seems small and harmless, yet it settles deep in the heart and poisons. We swallow it, and it nourishes everything bitter in us.
The lazy worker and the destroyer are cousins, really. Both abandon what they've been given. One wastes it slowly, the other breaks it quickly, but the result is the same ruin.
In ancient times, a strong tower was where the city turned when enemies came—a place of refuge. The Lord's name is just that: a refuge where we are kept safe. Run there.
How tragic—the wealthy man believes his gold builds an unscalable wall, yet it's only imagination. His riches are an illusion of safety, and he'll wake too late to that truth.
Pride whispers lies: 'You're invincible.' And we believe it—until we fall. But humility listens to God and stands firm. The humble stand before honor; the proud before ruin.
To speak before listening is to build without looking at the ground. You'll likely build on quicksand and shame yourself with your own hasty words.
A quiet spirit—even in sickness—carries us through. But a broken spirit is a terrible weight. Guard your heart; its strength matters more than the body's comfort.
The discerning heart and the wise ear both lean forward to understand. They hunger for truth the way a thirsty man seeks water. They grow wiser because they listen.
A gift in the hand opens doors and clears the way forward. It's not about bribing—it's about recognizing the small grace of generosity. What we offer makes room for us.
The first voice in a dispute seems right—we believe him because we heard him first. But patience waits for the other side. Truth is not finished until all voices have been heard.
In ancient Israel, disputes were settled by casting lots—trusting God to decide through that sacred act. When human pride runs too hot, sometimes we must step back and let the Lord judge.
A brother's anger is harder to heal than a city's walls are to breach. Once offense comes between family, the fortress of resentment rises high and fast. Guard fraternity as treasure.
We eat what we speak. Our words are a harvest we reap from our own mouths. Sow kind words and you taste kindness. Sow bitterness and you sup on your own poison.
Death and life hang on the tongue—not as fancy metaphor, but as plain truth. The tongue holds power to bless or curse, to heal or wound. Speak as one who knows this weight.
A good wife is a treasure and a gift from the Lord's hand. To find such a companion is to receive grace itself—a kindness from God that blesses all of life.
The poor must beg because they have nothing; the rich can afford to be harsh because they feel secure. Yet the Lord hears the cry of the weak and despises the hard heart of the strong.

Readers today hear an echo in this verse: in a world of many acquaintances and shallow bonds, a true friend—one who stays close as a brother—is rarer and more precious than ever. Such friendship is worth more than a full circle of pleasant company.

A person who keeps their word and walks straight, even in poverty, holds more honor than one who speaks smoothly but twists the truth. Integrity is a kind of wealth no amount of silver can buy or take away.
Zeal that runs faster than understanding is like starting a journey at a sprint—we charge ahead, miss the path, and end up lost. The wisest move is to look, listen, and learn before we rush forward.
When a person's own folly ruins their way, sometimes they grow angry at God instead of at themselves. How often do we blame heaven for what our own choices have wrought?
Money draws crowds like honey draws bees, but when the honey is gone, so are the bees. The poor learn early which friendships are real—they are the ones who stay when there is nothing to gain.
A false witness carries a debt that cannot be paid except by suffering. The law itself—the very order God built into the world—will collect what was owed. Lies have their own reckoning.
Notice who gathers around a person of influence or wealth—they come with their hands open and their hearts calculating. A gift buys presence, not affection; favor buys flattery, not friendship.

The poor person watches even family slip away, despite calling after them. Such loneliness teaches a hard lesson: kinship is not enough if there is no kindness. Yet this is also where the Lord finds His own.
To love wisdom is to love yourself well—not in pride, but in the deep care a shepherd shows the flock. Understanding becomes its own reward; it opens doors to goodness we never knew were there.
The liar speaks twice—once with the lie, and again in the judgment that follows. There is no escape hatch; the path of falsehood always ends in ruin, whether quickly or slowly.
A fool in luxury is a creature out of place—as wrongly fitted as a servant ruling over princes. Some people simply lack the judgment to carry what they've been given.

A person of discernment does not rush to anger—they think first and choose later. To let an offense pass when you have the right to retaliate: this is the glory of a restrained heart, the truest strength.
A king's anger shakes like a lion's roar; his favor falls gentle as morning dew on dry grass. The same ruler can bring ruin or renewal—how blessed are those under a hand that chooses mercy.
A foolish child is a father's deepest sorrow, and a wife's endless complaints wear grooves in the heart like water on stone. Home was meant to be a refuge, not a battlefield.
Property passes down through generations, but a wise and careful wife—one who fears the Lord and tends the home with grace—is a gift only God can give. She is worth more than any inheritance.
Sloth is a kind of sleep, and the sleeper wakes to find the cupboard bare and the body weak. Laziness does not seem so costly at first—until hunger cries and there is nothing left to eat.
To keep God's commandment is to keep your own soul—to guard the one thing that truly matters. Contempt, on the other hand, is a road that ends only in death.
When you give to the poor, you are lending directly to the Lord—what a strange and glorious bookkeeping! He does not forget a kindness shown in His name and will repay with interest only He can give.
Discipline a child while there is still hope, while the heart is still soft and teachable. To withhold correction is to wish them harm; to correct in love is to offer them a future.
A person quick to rage pays a steep price—and if you rush in to rescue them each time, you become trapped in the same cycle. Some lessons must be learned in the fire.
Listen closely to counsel; let others' wisdom shape your path. The one who heeds this instruction will find, when age comes, that they have walked into blessing, not wandering.
Our hearts are full of plans—careful schemes, hopes, dreams. Yet the Lord's purpose stands alone, bending all our plotting toward His will. We are never truly in charge, and what a relief that is.
What makes a person truly admirable is kindness—the willingness to give when no return is promised. And a poor honest soul outweighs a rich liar; one has their soul intact.

Readers today hear an echo in this: to reverence the Lord leads toward life itself—not mere survival, but a life that rests in contentment, safe from the storms that wreck others. How many sleepless nights does the frightened heart spend, while the trusting one rests?
The sluggard dips his hand in the dish but cannot summon the will to lift it to his mouth—a picture of laziness so deep it becomes almost paralysis. Some prisons are locked from the inside.
Strike a scoffer, and the naive will learn caution; correct one who understands, and they will grow wiser still. Different people need different teachers; some learn by watching, others by listening.
To rob your father and drive away your mother is to burn the very house that sheltered you. Such a child brings shame upon themselves—a reproach that follows through the years and marks the soul.
Stop listening to wisdom, and your feet will wander from the path. The voice that once guided you becomes fainter and fainter until you realize you have lost your way entirely.
A corrupt witness makes a mockery of justice, laughing at the truth while speaking lies. And the wicked—they swallow iniquity as naturally as breathing, never pausing to feel its weight.
Judgment is already prepared for scoffers; it hangs like a sword waiting to fall. The fool who mocks wisdom will learn its truth the hard way—written upon their back in suffering.

I've seen it happen—a man thinks a drink or two will ease his troubles, but it mocks him instead. You'd think we'd learn that whatever promises the bottle, the One who made us promises something steadier.
Authority carries weight, yes—but a king's wrath is a warning we can understand. When we provoke power unjustly, we bet our own breath on foolishness.
I've noticed the honorable ones walk past the quarrel. They don't need to prove themselves in every squabble. The fool, though—he can't help himself, always itching for the next fight.

Winter comes to every field. The sluggard sees the cold and stays home—then wonders in harvest why his hands are empty. The Lord teaches through seasons: work when the hour comes, or hunger teaches instead.
A man's heart holds water too deep for him to see the bottom. But someone of real understanding—that one knows how to draw the truth up into the light where it can be seen.
Everyone speaks of their great love—loyalty is easy to promise. But find the soul who keeps their word when it costs? That one you hold close. That's rare as dawn.

A righteous life isn't a solo song—it echoes forward into the lives of those who come after. His children inherit not gold, but something steadier: the proof that integrity pays, even when nobody's watching.
A wise king sees rightly—his eyes are windows to justice. When he looks, evil scatters like shadows at sunrise. This is how the Lord meant authority to work: sight that heals.
Nobody can stand and say it honestly—'My heart is pure.' This verse is a question that folds us forward: if I can't claim it, where do I turn? The answer waits in mercy, not in our own scrubbing.
A false weight and a false measure—both rob someone. The Lord hates them both. He cares about small things: honesty in commerce, truth in the everyday transactions where we meet one another.

Watch a child at play and you see their heart made visible—not in words, but in the work of their hands, the choices they make when they think nobody's keeping score. Character begins early and shows early.
Both the ear and the eye come from the Lord's hand. This is a small prayer of gratitude: that we hear, that we see, that these gifts let us taste the world He made. Don't take them for granted.
There's a love of sleep that eats a life. The one who opens his eyes and rises finds himself satisfied—not rich, maybe, but fed. There's dignity in waking to your own work.

'No good, no good,' the buyer says, talking the price down with a sorrowful face. But once he leaves the gate, he brags about his bargain. I've learned to smile at this—it's human nature, and the Lord knows it.
Gold and rubies fill the world—treasures you can name and count. But wise speech, true knowledge from a faithful heart? That's the rare thing. That's what holds real weight.

When a man signs a pledge for a stranger or binds himself for a woman of loose ways, take his coat—hold it as security. This is wisdom's hard hand: protect the foolish from themselves by letting consequence speak.
Dishonest gain tastes sweet going down—but the mouth fills with gravel when you chew. The Lord made our consciences to work like this: pleasure turns to ash when it's built on wrong.
Plans thrive when many voices speak into them. Even in battle, wise counsel steadies the way. The Lord puts counselors around us—not to mock our struggles, but to light the path.
A gossip reveals secrets and opens wide his lips—you can hear him coming. Distance yourself kindly from such a one. There's no small betrayal; every word matters to someone.

To curse father or mother is to curse the ones through whom life came. His lamp goes out in darkness—the consequence is built into the act itself. Honor your parents: the Lord insists on it because He knows what breaks us.
An inheritance grabbed fast, won in haste, won't stand. Real blessing grows in time and trust. The Lord's gifts to us are the same—deeper when received with patience than when seized.
'I'll pay them back,' we say when we're hurt. But the Lord asks us to wait—to stay our hand and let Him. This is where faith becomes real, not in words but in the hardest silence.
False weights again—the Lord returns to this. He hates dishonest scales. Why? Because He loves the widow and the orphan, the ones cheated by a thumb on the scale. His justice is precise and personal.
A man's steps come from the Lord. So how can he understand his own path while he's still walking it? There's humility in this—trust in a guide you cannot fully see. That's where faith begins.
We rush to make a vow—promise something rashly in the heat of devotion. Then later we hesitate, unsure. A trap lies there. Better to think first, speak second, than to trap yourself with hasty words.
A wise king puts the wicked to the wheel—drives through them like chaff. This is strength used rightly: not for pride, but to protect the innocent. Real power serves the vulnerable.

The Lord's lamp searches our inner rooms—this is what readers today hear as an echo: Jesus knowing us fully, seeing past our surface to the true heart. There's terror in it, yes. But also welcome. He sees and loves anyway.
Love and faithfulness guard a king—not armies, but the deeper forces. His throne stands when it rests on love. The same is true for any life: we endure when we are rooted in true affection.

Young men glory in their strength, strong arms and tireless legs. Old men wear their gray hair like a crown—that's the splendor of years survived, wisdom earned hard. Both are honored here; both have their season.

Wounds and blows cleanse away evil—this is speaking of conscience, discipline, consequences that teach. The Lord sometimes uses hardship to purge us of what poisons us from within. Even pain can be a mercy.
A king's heart in the Lord's hand—like water finding its course. Even those who seem most powerful are, in His mercy, already held and turned toward His purpose. This is both humbling and consoling.
How easy it is to think our own path is the only reasonable one. We see our motives kindly; the Lord sees them plainly. His weighing is not cruel—it is what sets us free from our own deceit.

Right living and fair dealing please the Lord far more than incense burned with a divided heart. He wants us, not our religious performance. That's a hard mercy to accept when we're used to earning favor.
Arrogance broadcasts itself—a lifted chin, a hard heart. The wicked wear their sin like a lamp, all light and no warmth. The Lord sees it plainly; we need not pretend we don't.
Steady work builds; hurry squanders. The sluggard's haste is born of fear, the diligent's patience of trust. I've seen both in my years. The patient one sleeps better.
Lies and wealth gathered by deception have a mist about them—never solid, always slipping away. Those who build on falsehood are building for their own undoing.
The violence of the wicked drags them away, not by chance but by their refusal to walk the narrow way. They choose their own exile when righteousness stands plainly offered.
The guilty twists and turns, always covering. The innocent walks a straight line—not because the way is easy, but because they have nothing to hide. There's a deep freedom in honesty.
A corner of the housetop—cold, alone, but peaceable. Better that solitude than the constant heat of contention. Peace, even if small, is itself a treasure worth guarding.
The wicked soul hungers for harm and finds no mercy to give. What we crave, we become. A hard truth—but it shows us we're not bound by our desires if we turn toward grace.
The mocker learns by watching consequences; the wise learns by receiving instruction. Both paths teach, but one is kinder. The wise know how to hear; that's half the battle.

The Righteous One—the Lord—sees every wicked home and will not let its harm stand forever. His attention to injustice is part of His faithfulness, not cruelty. That vigilance is on behalf of the afflicted.
When we stop our ears to the poor, we build our own silence. One day our cry will go unanswered by the very mercy we withheld. What we sow in hardness, we reap in loneliness.
A quiet gift can turn anger aside. Sometimes, a small kindness placed unseen does what words never could. Yet a bribe covers wickedness; the motive matters as much as the gesture.
Justice brings joy to the righteous—it restores the broken world a little. For those who work iniquity, it is ruin. The same act splits their worlds because they've chosen opposite sides.
Wander from understanding and you end among the dead, without even knowing it until it's too late. The assembly of the departed—those who chose foolishness—is not a place we should take lightly.

Those who chase pleasure and wine find their coffers empty—not by accident, but by the nature of the chase itself. Emptiness pursues the one who pursues emptiness. The rich are those who know what matters.

The wicked stands in place of the righteous sometimes—suffering consequences the faithful might have borne. It's not fortune but the Lord's mysterious justice, protecting His own in ways we seldom fully understand.
Better a desert—bare, solitary, but quiet—than endless strife. There's wisdom in knowing when silence is better than company, when alone is better than beside someone who will not be at peace.

The wise gather precious things—treasure and oil, the necessities—and keep them. The fool, even in plenty, devours and wastes. The difference lies in restraint and the awareness that today's store may be tomorrow's need.

Pursue rightness and mercy—chase after them—and life itself comes to you. Not as a bargain struck, but as the natural fruit of walking toward the Lord's own heart. Honor follows righteousness like a shadow.
Wisdom can scale walls the strong cannot. It reaches what brute force never will. The mighty cities, for all their confidence, fall to the wise. This is how the kingdom of God works.

Guard your mouth and tongue as you would guard your own soul—because you are. Words spoken in anger or haste breed troubles that take a lifetime to bury. Silence, chosen rightly, is a form of bravery.
The scoffer's name is his nature—his pride wears like a skin he thinks honors him. He works with arrogance as his tool, not seeing that his own blindness is his undoing.
The sluggard's desire kills him—he craves rest, comfort, ease, but his hands won't move to earn them. His own longing, unfed by effort, becomes the slow knife that undoes him.
Some covet all day long, grasping at what belongs to others. The righteous give and hold nothing back—not from scarcity, but from abundance of heart. That generosity is its own wealth.

The wicked's sacrifice is an abomination—and how much worse when the mind behind it is twisted. The Lord reads the heart, not the gift. Our offerings mean nothing if they don't come from cleaned hands.
A false witness perishes; one who listens—truly listens—speaks as though into eternity. The word spoken by the truthful carries weight that echoes beyond this moment. That's the power of honesty.

The wicked harden their faces like stone, unmoved by shame or consequence. The upright, by contrast, are purposeful—their ways established not by stubbornness but by steady conviction in what's right.

No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel stands against the Lord. We can devise plans without end, but if they run counter to His will, they crumble. That's not a warning to be timid—it's an invitation to align ourselves with truth.

A horse is made ready for battle—we prepare, we plan, we do our part faithfully. But victory belongs to Yahweh alone. Our work matters; His sovereignty matters more. That paradox is where faith lives.

I've learned that the name we build—our reputation—shapes everything. When people trust your word, when they know you mean what you say, that's wealth no bank can steal. The Lord looks at the heart, and He builds us up through a lifetime of small faithfulnesses.

Rich and poor meet on the same ground—the Lord made them both. I've watched money make some people proud and others fearful, but the dust we came from silences both. What matters is that we meet each other with eyes open to God's hand on us all.

The wise see trouble coming and step aside; the fool wanders on and gets hurt. I've noticed it takes only a little humility to notice what's ahead—a hard word, a dangerous path, a temptation dressed up as opportunity. The prudent ask, 'Is this where God is calling me?'

Humility and reverence for the Lord—they're the real inheritance. I've seen how true honor and a life worth living flow from fearing God first, not from chasing riches. The Lord never skimps when He gives to those who seek Him with a quiet heart.

The path of wickedness is trapped and thorny, and those who walk it will be cut. Yet here's the grace: we can guard our souls by staying close to God and turning away. A tender conscience is a gift worth more than comfort.

Training a child in 'the way he should go'—I've come to understand that means knowing each one, not forcing them all the same way. The Lord shapes each person uniquely, and our job is to guide them toward Him with gentleness and consistency. Years later, when they're grown and the world tugs at them, they remember.

Debt is a chain, plain and simple—the lender holds power over the borrower. I've watched good people struggle under obligations they couldn't keep, losing peace in the process. The Lord calls us to live within our means and help others do the same.

What we sow, we reap—wickedness planted bears a bitter crop. Yet notice: the fury itself gets destroyed, not just the one who sowed it. The Lord's justice is real, and it even limits the damage a wicked person can keep doing.

A generous eye sees the need and blesses freely. It's not the size of the gift that matters—it's the open hand and the turned heart. I've noticed the generous are often the most content; there's a quiet joy in sharing.

Remove the mocker, and quarrels lose their fuel. I've learned that some people feed on contention and stir up strife for its own sake. Peace-making sometimes means letting go of those who won't stop stirring the pot.

A pure heart speaks gracefully—one flows from the other. I've watched people with clean consciences before the Lord win trust and favor naturally. Grace isn't manipulation; it's the overflow of a heart at peace with God.

The Lord watches over knowledge and protects true wisdom, while lies unravel. I've seen deceivers trip themselves up; their words contradict and people stop trusting them. But those who speak truth find it upheld, even when it costs them.

The lazy person invents grand excuses for inaction—there's always a lion in the road. I've noticed laziness isn't rest; it's restlessness dressed as caution. The Lord calls us to work faithfully, not to hide behind invented fears.

The seductive path leads deep, and those who are already under God's judgment find themselves trapped there. I've watched people mistake desire for destiny and lose much in the process. The Lord sets boundaries to protect us, not to diminish us.

Foolishness is natural to the young heart; wise training helps turn it away. I've learned that correction given with love, not anger, helps a young person see. The goal isn't to crush the spirit but to guide it toward wisdom.

Exploitation—whether of the poor for profit or flattery of the rich for favor—leads to ruin. I've noticed the Lord hates a double standard. Those who use others end up hollow, no matter what they gain.

Here the wise teacher calls us to listen carefully and take it to heart. I've learned that wisdom isn't absorbed passively; it requires turning our ear, attending closely, and letting it reshape our thinking. The Lord speaks through many voices when we're humble enough to hear.

When wisdom lives in you, it becomes ready on your lips—no fumbling, no pretense. I've noticed it's hard to speak what you haven't truly believed; and lovely when truth flows from a heart that's already tasted it.

All this teaching points to one end: that we trust the Lord ourselves. I've learned that the deepest wisdom always brings us back to Him—not to rules or pride, but to reliance on the One who holds all things.

The teacher offers thirty counsels—a treasury of wisdom tested by time and experience. I've found that multiple reflections on the same truths help them settle deeper in the soul. Repetition, when it carries real weight, is a kindness.

Sound answers come from grounding in truth and reliable words. I've learned that when others come asking, the one who knows God's mind can answer with confidence and humility both. That's the gift of studying under those who've walked with Him.

Don't exploit the poor because they have no defense. I've noticed how easy it is for strength to crush weakness when we're not watching our hearts. The Lord has a special tenderness toward the vulnerable, and He calls us to have it too.
The Lord Himself becomes the advocate for the poor and powerless. I've seen how those who exploit others—even in small, 'legal' ways—end up losing everything. His justice is patient but sure.

A hot-tempered friend teaches you rage; an angry companion rehearses blame. I've learned the hard way that close friendships shape us—not by instruction, but by osmosis. Choose company that's becoming what you want to be.

You become like those you walk with—absorbing their habits, their patterns of thought, their way of handling the world. I've noticed people don't change all at once; they drift slowly toward the company they keep. Protect your soul by choosing wisely.

Don't pledge yourself as collateral for someone else's debt—you'll be bound by another's choices. I've watched good intentions lead to financial ruin this way. The Lord calls us to be generous, but not to surrender our discernment.

If you can't pay, the creditor will take what little you have—even your bed, your shelter. I've learned this isn't just about money; it's about the consequences of binding ourselves to promises we can't keep. Live carefully and honestly.

The ancient boundary stone marks what your fathers set—the inheritance and order they preserved. Don't move it—it's a law deeper than comfort. I've noticed the Lord honors those who keep faith with what's been given, not just what's convenient.

Readers today hear an echo in this verse: the person whose work shows true skill rises, not by luck or favor, but by faithful doing. We still see this—the diligent person finds their way to greater responsibility. The Lord honors excellence that comes from a humble heart.

When you're invited to the table of someone powerful, the invitation carries a trap disguised as a privilege. It's easy to forget yourself and become what you think he wants you to be—losing your own heart in the process.

A sharp word, that—put a knife to your throat. It's not literal violence, but a call to ruthless honesty about your own appetites. If you know yourself to be someone who wants more than is good for you, then guard that hunger like your life depends on it.

The finer the spread, the easier it is to forget what you actually need. Deceitful food looks more generous than it is—it promises something it cannot give. There's always a cost hidden beneath the flattery.
The race to be rich exhausts the soul and clouds the mind. Wisdom isn't found in the sweat—it's found in knowing when to stop, when to rest, and what you actually own versus what merely owns you.

I've watched wealth and opportunity flutter away from the most grasping hands. The things we fix our eyes on most fiercely are often the ones that slip away fastest—like an eagle vanishing into the sky. Hold the good things loosely.

A stingy eye—that's a window into a stingy heart. Someone who grudges every crumb he shares will poison the meal with resentment. The gift becomes a transaction, and you'll leave hungrier than when you came.

As he thinks about the cost, so he is—those words matter more than they sound. A man who measures everything by what it drains is already depleted. His hospitality is false because his heart cannot afford genuine generosity.

What tastes good going down can poison you once it's inside. Not because the food is bad, but because you realize too late what the host was actually offering—a transaction disguised as kindness. Your own words of thanks become bitter in your mouth.

There's a hard wisdom in knowing when to be silent. The fool won't receive your wisdom—he'll turn it into evidence against you. Sometimes the kindest thing is to preserve your words for soil that can actually receive them.

The ancient boundary stone marks what is not yours. In land law, moving it was theft against the living and dishonor to the dead. The poor have little—the fatherless have nothing—so the boundary matters doubly to those with no strength to defend it.

The Lord pleads for the fatherless. That's not a weakness in God—it's His fierce, protective love. When you respect that boundary and protect the defenseless, you're answering to the One who will settle every score on their behalf.

The heart and the ears—both must turn toward learning. Instruction doesn't happen in your head alone; it lives in your willingness to listen again and again, even when you think you already know. That humble attention is where wisdom begins.

A difficult verse for gentler times, but the heart of it endures: correction is an act of love, not cruelty. A parent who never redirects abandons a child to his own ruin. The discomfort of correction can save a life.
Sheol is the grave, the great forgetting. The proverb isn't about punishment but redemption—discipline keeps the soul alive, awake, present to life and to God. It's the parent's hard mercy.

The father's joy runs deep when his child's heart turns wise. There's no greater reward for a parent—no amount of wealth or reputation comes close. A wise child is the father's vindication and his hope.

My heart will rejoice when your lips speak what is right. Words matter because they show what's in the heart. A child whose speech aligns with truth brings their father more joy than any accomplishment.
Don't envy the sinner—that's the first step. The second is to fear the Lord all day long, to keep turning your gaze back. Fear here means awe and trust, the only antidote to the poison of envy.
There is a future hope. The sinner's gain will crumble, but the faithful one's hope will never be severed. In the end, the faithful inherit something real—not the fool's glitter, but true life.
Keep your heart on the right path—that's where the listening happens. It's not about perfection but about direction, about choosing alignment with wisdom again and again, especially when you slip.
The drunk and the glutton—those who live for excess and appetite rather than purpose. They're not wicked, but they've made themselves small and weak, slaves to desires that will never satisfy.

Poverty is the natural end of a life given over to excess—not as punishment, but as simple harvest. The man who will not discipline his appetites loses everything. Drowsiness clothes him in rags because he cannot even rise to defend himself.

Honor your father and your mother—it's the law carved in stone. When your mother is old and small, that's when the test comes true. What you do for her then is what your children will remember and learn.

Buy the truth—it costs something. Wisdom, discipline, understanding—these are not free gifts that arrive without effort. But they're worth more than silver, and once purchased, never to be sold for any price.

A father can do nothing with his life that compares to fathering a wise child. That child becomes his joy, his legacy, his vindication. The proverb speaks to both father and child—to raise one and to become one.
Let your father and mother rejoice—that's the fruit of your becoming wise. Your righteousness is the only gift they want. Everything you give them pales beside the joy of seeing you alive in truth.

Give me your heart—that's what the father asks. Not just your obedience or your success, but your actual self, your desires, your attention. Let your eyes keep in my ways means living where you can be seen and corrected by one who loves you.

A prostitute is a deep pit because she offers what looks like intimacy but leads to entanglement and loss of self. The wayward wife is the same trap in a different form—both rob a man of his substance and his soul.

She lies in wait like a robber. That predatory image is clear—this isn't about a woman's worth, but about a particular path of action that steals men away. She increases the unfaithful because she uses deception as her weapon.

Who has woe?—a series of questions with answers written in every face marked by excess. The drunk's sorrow is not hidden; it's inscribed in bloodshot eyes and bruises. The proverb speaks to those who can read the signs.
Those who seek out wine, who stay long at it—they're hunting for something. But what the bottle promises and what it delivers are not the same. The search itself becomes the trap.

Don't even look at it—that's the strength of the warning. When it's red and sparkles, it's at its most seductive, most dangerous. Prevention is wiser than repentance. The temptation itself is where the battle is won or lost.
In the end, it bites like a snake—the smooth beginning turns vicious. What seemed like friendship becomes poison. Those who pursue it learn too late that what felt like reward was always venom.

Your eyes see strange things, your mind spins with confusion—the loss of clarity is part of the cost. The drunk doesn't just lose control; he loses his grip on what's real. The shame is that he chose this blindness.

He lies on the rigging of a ship in a storm—completely unaware of danger, completely helpless. The drunk is in the same peril but cannot feel it. That's the mercy God doesn't grant: to pass through danger and sleep through it.

They hit me and I don't feel it—readers today hear an echo of the addict's blindness. How many times does someone have to wake up and decide to chase the same thing again? This verse traces the saddest cycle: oblivion that feels like freedom, until it isn't.

It's easy to be drawn in by the world's shine—to wonder what we're missing when others seem to have everything. But look closer: envy is its own prison. The Lord calls us away from that hunger, toward something steadier.

Words reveal the heart. What we say—and what we plot in silence—shows who we're becoming. The wise notice this and step back. I've learned that quiet listening teaches me more than a room full of smooth talkers.

A house built on sand looks fine until the rain comes. But wisdom lays a different kind of foundation—not shortcuts or luck, but patient understanding of how things truly work. Jesus is the cornerstone I keep coming back to.

Knowledge fills the house with treasure—not gold, but the real riches: peace in hard seasons, good counsel for the next generation, a clear conscience. I've seen homes without much money overflow with these things.

Power without wisdom is a drunk with a sword. But a wise person—one who thinks before acting, who listens before speaking—moves through the world with real strength. It's a quiet kind of strength, but it lasts.

Even the best battle strategy fails without good counsel. Pride wants to decide alone, but the Lord often whispers through the voices of others—a friend's warning, a stranger's question that makes you think. Wise people listen.

The gate was where Israel's elders judged, where wisdom spoke to the community. A fool has no voice there because foolishness has nothing to offer when it counts. Wisdom stays quiet until there's something true to say.

You become what you plot. The person who spends hours planning mischief has already changed inside—they're not the same as they were before. The name fits because the deed has already taken root in the heart.

Folly isn't just foolishness—it's sin, which means it's a turning away from God's design. And those who mock the good? They find themselves alone eventually. Mockery has a hollow ring that others hear before they hear the words.

Trouble is a measure. When pressure comes, we see what we're truly made of. If we fold like paper, our inner strength was smaller than we thought. But if we've been rooted in something steady—in the Lord—trouble finds firm ground.

This is about the harvest slaves being led to execution, the condemned who stumble toward judgment. Rescue them—intervene when you can. The Lord takes this personally. It's one of wisdom's clearest commands: speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves.

We can't pretend ignorance before God. 'We didn't know'—but He weighs the heart; He sees what we chose not to see. And He will judge not by excuses but by what we actually did. That settles something in me—I can't hide from Him, so why would I try?

Honey speaks for sweetness—taste something good and you understand good. My son, the writer says, eat it. Know wisdom by its fruit, by its flavor on your tongue. There's an invitation here: come and see that the Lord is good.

When you find wisdom, you've found a future. Your hope won't be cut off—that's a promise built into the kind of life wisdom shapes. It's not wealth or fame, but something deeper: a hope that carries you through.

The righteous person's home, their place of rest—don't scheme against it. There's something sacred about a good person's peace, about the small sanctuary they've made. The Lord sees when someone tries to steal that.

Seven times—an old number of fullness. The righteous person falls and falls and falls, but rises each time. That's the difference between them and the wicked: not that they don't fall, but that they get back up. One calamity overthrows the wicked because they had no root.

When an enemy falls, something in us wants to cheer. But hold that back. Gloating has a cost—it hardens the heart and blocks grace. The Lord Himself doesn't gloat over the fallen; He grieves them. That's the measure I want to live up to.
God sees your joy in another's downfall, and it displeases Him. He may turn His patience away—from the fallen enemy, but also from you, the one who gloated. Mercy ends when pride takes over.

Don't fret. Don't be envious. These two commands pair up—they're the same struggle. It's the ache of watching the world seem to reward the wrong people. But fretting changes nothing; it only poisons you from inside.

No reward for evil—that's the long view. Their lamp goes out. I've watched people chase gain through harm, and yes, they accumulate things for a while. But it never lasts. The darkness always catches up.

Fear the Lord and honor the king—two kinds of respect, both rooted in the same posture. Don't join the rebels, the ones who think they can remake everything to suit themselves. Rebellion has its own weight.

Calamity rises suddenly for the rebellious. They plot and plan, but destruction comes when they don't expect it. Who knows what forms it will take? That's the terror of opposing God and authority alike.

A new collection of wisdom sayings begins here. And the first word: partiality in judgment is not good. A judge favoring the rich or the connected has already abandoned the law. Justice must be blind to anything but truth.

To call the guilty righteous is perversion. The judge who does this earns curses—peoples rise against him, nations hold him in contempt. You can't lie about judgment without the whole world knowing you're a fool.

But for those who convict the guilty—who speak truth even when it costs—blessing falls. This is the flip side: honesty draws the favor of the good. It goes well with them because they've aligned themselves with righteousness.

An honest answer is like a kiss on the lips—tenderness, acceptance, a sign of affection. The person who speaks truth without cruelty, who looks you in the eye and tells you what's real, gives you a gift. That's intimacy.

Put your work in order before you build your house. Plant the fields, establish what sustains you, then build the home. There's a right order to things—we ignore it to our cost. The foundation must be laid before the walls go up.

Don't testify falsely against someone, not even someone you dislike. Lies in court are lies before God. Your lips can lift someone up or destroy them—use that power carefully. The Lord sees what you swear to.

'I will do to him as he's done to me'—revenge at eye-level. But that's not the way. The moment you match harm for harm, you've become what you hated. Jesus teaches us a different mathematics: forgive seventy times seven.

The speaker walks past a sluggard's field—a real place, a real example. He stops to look and learn. This is how wisdom often comes: not from books alone, but from pausing to observe what neglect creates.
Thorns, nettles, broken walls—a landscape of abandonment. When no one tends the work, nature reclaims it fast. There's a parable in every weed-choked field about what happens when we stop caring.
The speaker saw, considered well, and learned. That's the practice of wisdom: look carefully, think deeply, let the lesson sink in. One sluggard's ruin becomes a classroom for the wise.

A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of hands—the repetition makes you hear the voice: small choices, easy justifications, a dozen reasons why not today. But these small indulgences compound.

Poverty comes as a robber, want as an armed man—readers today hear an echo in sudden loss, in plans derailed by neglect, in how small delays become large holes. As of 2026-10, I see this: the sluggard wakes to find that time has stolen everything he put off building.

See how the Lord preserves wisdom through human hands—Hezekiah's scribes copied these very words, passing Solomon's counsel down the centuries. We too are scribes of grace, passing on what we've learned. Every time we write down what God has taught us, we're part of that long chain of faithful preservation.

The Lord keeps His counsel—some mysteries we'll never know this side of heaven, and that's His good right. But what a gift He gives kings and all of us: the joy of searching, of asking, of understanding what we can. The searching itself draws us closer to Him.

A king's heart holds depths we cannot fathom—much like God Himself. But notice: the proverb calls us to humility, not cynicism. When we bow before what we cannot understand, we leave room for the Spirit to work in ways our minds never could have mapped.

The refiner knows which ore becomes the pure metal—and which is waste. The Lord refines us too, burning away what doesn't belong so we emerge more precious. If your life feels hot just now, remember: the fire is meant to make you more, not less.

Wickedness corrupts everything it touches—a truth every leader learns the hard way. Remove the poison and the whole thing stabilizes. In our own hearts, Jesus is the one who removes what shouldn't be there, making us steady and just.

We're all tempted to claim a place we haven't been given—to speak up before we're called, to reach beyond our station. The plain truth: self-promotion rarely goes where we hope. Humility, meanwhile, lets God lift us in His time, not ours.

There's a kind of public shame that cuts deep—being diminished before those we want to impress. How much better to be surprised by honor we didn't seek. This is why humility isn't weakness; it's wisdom that protects our dignity by leaving room for grace to work.

Rushing to court because you're angry now? Wait. The neighbor who shamed you has a story too, and the law moves slowly. Before you bring charges, ask yourself if you'll regret this when you're thinking straight. Nine times out of ten, time reveals what haste would hide.

Work it out between you two. Take the offense to the person, not to everyone else. Jesus calls us to this kind of courage—the quiet kind, where you face another soul and seek peace rather than vindication.

Once you betray a confidence, you can never call it back. The listener leaves bearing a wrong judgment, the betrayed person learns not to trust you, and your own name carries a stain. Guard the secrets people tell you like they're sacred ground.

A word fitly spoken—not loud, not frequent, but *right*—catches light like gold and silver. I've never forgotten certain words spoken over me years ago, still gleaming. The Lord gives some of us the gift of timing and clarity. When you feel that stirring to speak, that might be it.

To receive correction gladly—as a gift, even—marks a teachable spirit. The wise person doesn't flinch when shown their fault; they see it as ornament, as beauty. If you've surrounded yourself with people willing to correct you gently, you're rich beyond measure.

Snow in harvest time refreshes and preserves—think of ancient ice brought down from mountains. A faithful messenger does the same: brings what's needed, arrives when promised, steadies the soul of those who sent them. Faithfulness in small duties is its own kind of miracle.

All talk, no follow-through—like clouds that promise rain but blow past dry. The Lord asks something harder of us: to be the kind of person whose word carries weight, whose promises actually arrive. It's not glamorous, but it changes everything.

Patience wears down resistance like water on stone—you'd be amazed. A soft tongue breaks bone; harshness only hardens. In our culture of quick anger, this is countercultural wisdom: let gentleness be your strength. The strong know they don't need to shout.

Even good things—honey, rest, pleasure—become poison if we lose measure. The Lord doesn't condemn sweetness; He teaches us to taste it wisely. Knowing when to stop, when enough is enough—that's a form of respect for both the gift and yourself.

Even good neighbors can tire of constant company—there's something about restraint that keeps a friendship fresh. Give people room to miss you. The friendships that last longest usually have space in them.

False witness is weaponry—a club, a sword, sharp arrow, all meant to wound. The person you're lying about cannot see it coming; the damage festers beneath the skin. The Lord sees. He remembers. And He grieves for those bearing false testimony.

Unreliable trust is excruciating—like stepping on a broken tooth or leaning on a twisted leg. When disaster comes, you need rock-solid ground. Choose your confidants carefully; be one yourself. This kind of faithfulness is rarer than gold.

Trying to cheer up someone in sorrow with careless song is like stripping away their coat in winter—it makes everything worse. Sometimes the kindest thing is silence, presence, a knowing look. The grieving don't need your music; they need your company.

Feed your enemy. Give him water when he's thirsty. This cuts against every impulse—yet the Lord said it first, and Jesus lived it. There's a dignity that transcends conflict; a compassion that disarms. When you refuse to let the divide become complete, you leave a door open.

Coals of fire on his head—not destruction, but the warmth of undeserved kindness that may soften a hard heart. The Lord promises the reward belongs to you, not to your enemy's judgment. When you bless those who curse you, you're trading places with Jesus.

North wind brings rain; backbiting brings an angry face. The natural law holds: as wind precedes the storm, so slander precedes conflict. See how the proverb mirrors the visible world to the invisible—cause and effect are just as sure.

A contentious spirit poisons the whole house—there's no room to breathe, nowhere to find rest. The lonely corner of a roof sounds desolate, yet it's preferable to constant conflict. Sometimes peace requires separation. The Lord doesn't call us to live in war.

Good news from afar—a letter from someone you love, word that a prayer was answered—arrives like cool water in the desert. In our impatient age, we forget how precious this is: news that refreshes the soul. The simplest message, truthfully sent, can sustain someone for days.

A righteous person who crumbles before wickedness—who stops fighting, who gives way—becomes useless to everyone who relied on them. Like a fouled well, they poison the hope of those who come seeking. Stand. The cost of compromise is always higher than we think.

Too much of anything good becomes unseemly—including the pursuit of honor for its own sake. Chasing your own glory is a hunger that never fills. But when you forget yourself in serving Christ, honor finds you quietly, without you asking. That's a grace worth waiting for.

Readers today hear an echo in this verse: how many of us have felt ourselves like a city without walls—no boundaries, no restraint, swept this way and that by every impulse and opinion? As of 2026-10, we see it everywhere, and the consequences are the same as in Solomon's day. Blessed are those who let the Lord be the gatekeeper of their hearts.

A fool praised is like the unnatural—snow that melts in summer's heat brings no good. When we honor those who walk in foolishness, we're working against the grain of God's ordered world, where wisdom alone deserves lifting up.

Words spoken against us in anger or malice—curses—don't stick to a soul that rests in the Lord's keeping. They flutter past like restless birds finding nowhere to land. I've learned not to hold every harsh word spoken; the Lord is my anchor.
A horse needs a whip, a donkey a bridle—these beasts understand only force. So too, some foolishness cannot be reached by gentle words alone; sometimes discipline is the only language that speaks.
When you meet a fool's foolish argument with foolishness of your own, you've lowered yourself to meet him on his ground. Stay steady; don't let him pull you down into his own empty thinking.

Yet sometimes a fool must hear the truth of his folly spoken back to him, or he'll convince himself—and others—that his way is wise. The two verses together teach us wisdom isn't a rule but a judgment call. Jesus knew when to rebuke and when to stay silent.
To send your word through a fool's mouth is to cripple your own message before it arrives. He will mangle it, corrupt it, or weaponize it; you'll have done violence to your own purpose.
A wise saying in a fool's mouth is like legs on a lame man—hanging loose, useless, almost mocking the truth it pretends to carry. The words sound right, but they serve no good end.
Giving honor to a fool is like loading a sling with a stone and hurling it at yourself—it will come back to harm you. Foolishness rewarded grows bolder, spreading mischief in its wake.
In a drunkard's hand, a thorn-stick becomes a weapon that wounds him as much as anyone. So a wise saying in a fool's mouth—meant to guide—becomes a wound. He misuses it.
Hiring a fool is hiring someone who will shoot arrows at random—striking your own interests as often as others'. When we put foolish people in places of influence, we invite chaos into our own work.

A dog returns to its vomit; a fool repeats his folly. The cycle is ugly and unchanging—until shame or grace breaks it. I've watched people circle the same mistakes their whole lives. What breaks the cycle is humility and the fear of the Lord.
A man convinced of his own wisdom is trapped where a fool is not—he won't seek help or see his need. At least a fool might one day reach for guidance. Pride is the hardest blindness to heal.

The sluggard invents lions in his path—catastrophes that don't exist—to justify lying in bed. Laziness speaks in the language of fear to excuse inaction. I've done this myself: feared what wasn't there to avoid what was.
A door on its hinge swings back and forth but goes nowhere. So the sluggard rolls from side to side on his bed—motion without purpose, busy yet doing nothing.

The sluggard's hand lies in the food dish, but his laziness is so complete he won't even lift it to his mouth. He starves himself while the bread is in reach. This is sloth at its most absurd and most sad.

The sluggard thinks himself wiser than seven wise counselors—he's convinced his idleness is actually prudence. Laziness breeds arrogance; they feed each other. The man who will not work believes he knows better than those who do.
Grabbing a dog's ears is folly—the dog will snap and bite. So meddling in a quarrel not yours is inviting anger, pain, and trouble. A peacemaker is different; a meddler is a fool.

A man who deceives his neighbor and then laughs it off as a joke is like a madman hurling torches, arrows, and death—seemingly playful but truly dangerous. His deception is a weapon, and his laughter is a lie. I've learned: a man who jokes about his dishonesty cannot be trusted.
A fire fed by wood keeps burning; starve it, and it dies. So quarrels live by fuel—words, gossip, rehashed wrongs. When we stop adding wood, the fire of conflict cannot stand.
A contentious man is like coals and embers—ready to ignite, always hot. He kindles strife wherever he goes; being near him is like standing near a fire waiting to catch you.

Whispered words sound soft and appealing—like sweets melting on the tongue—but they go deep into us. Gossip is pleasant to hear and poisonous to hold. I've watched it work its damage long after being spoken.
Silver polish on a broken pot looks rich on the outside but is still cracked underneath. A kind-sounding mouth hiding an evil heart is the same—beautiful words covering rottenness.
A malicious man wears his words like a mask, but underneath lives hatred. His lips deceive you; his heart betrays you. Watch not what a man says, but what he does over time.
When someone's speech is charming and smooth, test it more, not less. Seven abominations—complete, thorough evil—may hide behind that pleasant voice. Charm can be the greatest deception.

A malicious man may hide his wickedness for a time beneath clever words and deception, but he cannot hide it forever. In the end, in the assembly of truth, it will be exposed. God sees what we hide from men.

The one who digs a pit for others falls into it himself. He who rolls a stone toward others finds it returns to crush him. Wickedness is a trap that springs on its own builder. The Lord's justice is as certain as gravity.

A lying tongue hates the ones it wounds; flattery wields smooth words to ruin. Readers today hear an echo of this in a world drowning in half-truths and performance—we're taught that words matter less than outcomes, yet the tongue still cuts and corrupts. The Lord has always known: words reveal the heart.

How much fretting we do about next week, next month—and yet the Lord holds tomorrow. This verse isn't scolding us for planning; it's inviting us into a quieter kind of trust. Boasting dies away when we remember we don't even own the next hour.

Our own mouths are hungry for credit, aren't they? This gentle word asks us to step back and let our work speak. When we stay quiet about our own good, we find that others—and the Lord—see us more clearly than any speech could reveal us.

Stone is stone, sand is sand. But a fool's needling—a constant provocation—becomes an unbearable weight. Sometimes we bear the weightier trial not by might but by learning to recognize the fool's game and stepping back from it.

Anger is terrible; jealousy is something else entirely—it burns hotter and more irrationally. This is the warning of one who's watched jealousy consume people she loved. Turn from it before it takes hold.
