A friend who speaks truth, even hard truth, is choosing you—your growth—over your comfort. Hidden love never saved anyone; it's the courage to say the difficult thing that marks true friendship. Jesus showed us this on the cross.

Wounds from a friend are wounds with healing in them—they come from someone who sees your good and won't let you perish. The enemy's kisses are smooth lies. Know the difference; treasure the friend who wounds you for love.
Hunger and fullness reshape what we taste. When we're content, the sweetest thing can turn cloying; when we're starving, even bitter bread tastes like mercy. The Lord meets us where we are.

A bird belongs in her nest, and a man belongs with his family. Wandering leaves us exposed and lost. There is no stability, no true rest, in being everywhere except where the Lord called us to root down.

A friend's honest counsel is a perfume to the heart—it refreshes and steadies us. Not flattery, but the real voice of someone who knows us and wants our good. These are the conversations that make a life worth living.

When trouble comes, we learn who our neighbors really are—and that they matter more than distant family we've neglected. The Lord often hides His rescue in the ordinary faithfulness of someone nearby. Don't walk past them.

A child's faithfulness gives the parent an answer—not just comfort, but a true response to her worries and prayers. Your steadiness matters to those who love you. Walk wisely, and watch them find their strength renewed in you.

The prudent person sees the storm coming and moves to shelter; the simple one keeps walking and gets soaked. This isn't paranoia—it's the small wisdom of paying attention to what's real, then acting on it.

In the ancient Near East, taking garment-collateral was a real practice (see Exodus 22:26). This warns against pledging security for a stranger—and especially not for a wayward woman. Protect your household; entanglement in another's folly rarely ends well.

Good timing and a humble heart—these matter. A loud blessing first thing in the morning can feel like an intrusion or mockery, not warmth. The same kindness, offered gently and at the right moment, becomes a gift instead of a burden.

The steady drip of a contentious spirit—each complaint, each barb—wears you down like rain wearing stone. There is a corrosive quality to constant conflict that no single argument captures. Peace in the home is worth the small surrenders it requires.

You cannot control the wind, and you cannot squeeze oil by force—both slip away the harder you grip. Some temperaments and situations resist direct force. Wisdom sometimes means accepting what cannot be changed and finding a different path.

Iron sharpens iron—a real image of metalwork. One friend's character, his faithfulness, brings out the best in you by proximity and example. Seek friendships that sharpen you toward Christ, not smooth you down.

The fig tree is tended, not abandoned; care brings a harvest. Faithfulness in your work—whether for yourself or for those you serve—is not unnoticed. The Lord sees the one who tends what's been given to her.

Water shows us our face truly—not the version we imagine we project, but ourselves as we are. In the same way, our inner heart reveals who we really are. The masks slip away eventually. Better to tend the heart itself.

Sheol and Abaddon—death itself—never say 'enough.' Neither do our eyes, our wants, our grasping. The more we feed appetites without end, the more restless we become. Only Christ satisfies; everything else leaves us parched.

Fire tests metal and reveals its true worth. Praise—when it comes—tests a person too. How you receive it shows what's inside. Do you grow humble and grateful, or does praise feed a hidden pride? The furnace reveals the metal.

You can crush a fool into powder, and still the foolishness won't leave him. Some people, we learn, must choose wisdom themselves; our effort alone won't grind it into them. The Lord respects their choice even when it wounds us.

Know your flocks; pay attention to what's in your care. This is a call to attentiveness—to the work the Lord has given you, the people you shepherd, the resources you steward. Neglect kills what should flourish.

Riches fade; power passes to the next generation, then the next. What lasts is faithfulness, integrity, and a legacy of faith in Christ. Plant your life there, where nothing rusts or loses its throne.
The seasonal cycle of hay, new growth, and hillside harvests—the poem shifts here to the pastoral year. Each season has its work and gift. The Lord provides in rhythm; we receive in trust.

Lambs clothe us; goats become fields—every creature, every resource, flows from the Lord's hand into our need. Nothing is wasted; all provision is layered and purposeful. We are held by a generosity we often don't notice until we pause and look.

Readers today hear an echo of this in Christ's promise: 'I came that they may have life, and have it to the full' (John 10:10). The abundance of goat's milk feeds the family and the servants—a picture of grace overflowing to the last. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful He still pours out plenty beyond our need.
That roaring lion in verse 15 won't come near. Conscience, more than guards, keeps the wicked fleeing. The righteous walk with the Shepherd—what pursuer could match that?
When rebellion floods a house or kingdom, the chairs fill with chaos. I've watched it happen. One person of wisdom standing firm—that single anchor steadies everything.
A poor person who squeezes the poorer is like hail on a garden he claims to tend. The cruelty stings because it comes from someone who knows hunger. Christ sees it.
The law of God is not a cage but a door. Those who praise the wicked have lost the map. Those who keep it stand against that tide—unpopular, but standing on solid ground.

Seeking Yahweh—calling on His name as Israel did—opens the eyes. Evil men don't see justice because they're looking away from the source. The wicked are blind not from lack of sight but from turned hearts.
A person with nothing but integrity walks taller than the rich whose way is crooked. I've seen both. The poor one sleeps soundly; the rich one keeps counting.
A wise child keeps the law and brings honor home. A foolish one picks companions who dull the conscience—and shames the whole household with it.
The man who gathers wealth through biting interest is building a house on borrowed time. What he hoards, the merciful will inherit. God has a long memory and an eye for the poor.
If you turn deaf to the Word and then kneel to pray, the prayer itself becomes refuse. God listens to the heart that bends toward His law first. Everything else rings hollow.
The schemer who lures an honest soul into darkness falls into his own snare—this is how God's justice works. The blameless? They inherit the good the wrecker tried to steal.
The wealthy man thinks himself clever—his accounts dazzle him. But a poor person who truly understands? They see through the illusion. Riches can blind; wisdom sees clear.

When the righteous flourish, there's light and singing. When the wicked rise, good people go quiet—not from boldness fleeing, but from the shadow that falls. Watch the room's mood; it tells you who holds the moment.
The man who hides his sin stays trapped. But the one who confesses—names the thing in the light—finds mercy. This is how Jesus works: acknowledgment opens the door that secrets kept locked.
To fear the Lord—to hold His word and His heart in awe—brings blessing. To harden yourself against Him is to walk toward the cliff's edge. I've seen which path holds peace.

A wicked ruler is a roaring lion or charging bear—an image from the hunt, terror itself. Over the helpless, unarmored people, such a ruler is devastation. The picture is plain: absolute cruelty toward the defenseless.
The tyrant's lack of judgment is his own poison. But the leader who turns from ill-gotten gain—who refuses the easy steal—lives long and the people remember his name with gratitude.
A person stained with blood—haunted by the weight of what they've done—flees, always fleeing. Even when they stop running, no one will help them. The conscience is a relentless pursuer.
Walking without blame is not perfection—it's straightness of path, eyes on the mark. The crooked soul loses his footing suddenly: one moment of reckoning and the fall is complete.
Work the soil and you eat; chase the glittering thing and you starve. The law is patient and steady. Illusion is swift and consuming. Time tells which you believed.

A faithful person is surrounded by blessing—not always visible wealth, but the blessing of trust and fruitfulness. The one eager to be rich skips ahead of God's timeline and tumbles. There's a cost to the shortcut.
Favoritism is not good—everyone knows it. Yet a crumb of bread can bend the best of us. We're all closer to betrayal than we like to admit. The cost is so small, but the consequence is exile.
The stingy man chases riches so fast he doesn't see the trap. Poverty arrives, and he's unprepared. His own hurry has made him blind to the one thing he feared most.
A rebuke that's true, though it stings, brings later favor and respect. But flattery—pretty poison—wins the moment and leaves you hollow. I've lived long enough to know which friend you need.
Robbing your own mother or father, then saying 'It's no sin'—that's destruction dressed as reasonableness. You've made yourself a partner with the wrecker, the one who tears the house down.
Greed is a fire in the house—it burns up peace and sets neighbors against each other. Trust in Yahweh, by contrast, quiets the hunger and flourishes. I know which yields a better home.
A fool trusts only his own judgment—his own eyes, his own gut. But the one who walks in wisdom leans on God's counsel and is kept safe. Pride is a lonely place.
Give to the poor and you lack nothing that matters—your own soul stays open and grateful. Close your eyes to their need and you've invited the curse to your own door. God's math is sure.

Readers today hear an echo: when wickedness seems to reign unchallenged, good people lie low. But the Bible promises what we've seen: when evil finally breaks under its own weight, the righteous rise and flourish. Patience bearing fruit.

There's a mercy in the small warnings — the gentle tugs before the sudden collapse. When we stiffen our necks and refuse the voice calling us back, we place ourselves beyond rescue. How much better to bend a little now.

I've seen both: the lightness in a room when good leads, and the heaviness when corrupt hands hold the reins. The psalmists and prophets all knew it—the character of rulers ripples through the whole people like a stone in still water.
A son who treasures wisdom delights his father's heart; a son who chases empty pleasures empties his father's store and his own future. Both choices are loud and clear in what they cost.

A ruler who judges by what is right steadies a whole nation; one who takes a bribe is like wood rot—hidden at first, then the whole structure fails. The Lord Himself is called the Judge, and His kingdom stands forever on justice.

Flattery is a trap dressed up as kindness. The neighbor who always agrees, who oils your ego without speaking truth—he has already caught your foot. Watch for the friend who loves you enough to say what's hard.

Sin is a hunter; it stalks the wicked who run toward it and snares them by their own desire. But the righteous? They are free—free to rejoice, free to sing even in hard seasons, because their freedom isn't a captive thing.

The righteous are built differently inside—they have a stirring for the poor, a pull toward their cry. The wicked remain untouched, unmoved. It's not hard work for them to ignore; it's all they know. The righteous must work not to feel.

One mocker can kindle a whole city's chaos with a sneer and a word. But a wise soul steps back, breathes, and turns anger aside before it takes root. This is the quiet power that few admire but everyone eventually needs.

Take a foolish person to court and expect wisdom to settle the matter? No—the fool will rage or mock, and you'll leave exhausted with nothing resolved. Some disputes need the Lord's hand, not human judgment.

Those who thirst for bloodshed are repulsed by a person of real integrity—he stands as a rebuke just by breathing. They will hunt him, not because he's done them wrong, but because his uprightness condemns theirs by contrast.

A fool pours out every hot feeling, every rage, unfiltered. You know where you stand with him because he hides nothing. The wise man feels deeply too, but he brings himself under control—and that restraint is a kind of strength.

When a leader listens to lies, the whole circle rots. His officials become wicked not by personal choice alone, but by the permission and model he gives. One man's ear for falsehood corrupts an entire household.

The poor man and his oppressor have this strange meeting place: the Lord gives sight to both their eyes. He sees them equally, and this shared visibility means justice isn't far off—one day the oppressor will face his own doing.
A king who judges the poor fairly doesn't just do a good deed—he builds forever. His throne is stable because it rests on something solid: the gratitude and prayers of those he spared.
A child trained with loving correction learns wisdom; left to wander alone, he becomes a shame to his mother. This isn't cruelty—it's care. The hard word now saves him from a harder reckoning later.

The wicked flourish for a season, and each success seems to breed more wickedness in the people around them. But the righteous see it—they watch sin multiply and then watch it collapse. Patience in faith is its own reward.

A corrected child brings peace to his home and delight to his mother's soul. Not because he becomes perfect, but because he learns he is loved enough to be guided. That love, spoken firmly, creates a whole different kind of joy.

Where there is no word from the Lord—no vision, no revelation—people run wild, restless and untethered. But those who keep His law, who hold to what He has spoken, are blessed with something deep: a steadiness the lawless can never find.

Some souls are so hardened they can hear the truth clearly yet turn away as though you've said nothing. Words alone won't reach them—only experience, consequence, or grace. Don't exhaust yourself thinking correction alone will change such a heart.

A man who rushes to speak before thinking is in deeper trouble than any fool you might meet. At least a fool is honest about his foolishness; a hasty mouth hides behind the illusion of confidence. There's more hope for one who knows he is lost.

If you give a servant every comfort and never ask him to grow or take responsibility, you are raising him toward bitterness, not gratitude. True care sometimes means saying 'no,' asking more, and watching him become a man instead of staying a dependent child.

An angry man doesn't just lose his temper—he loses his way, pulling others into the current of his wrath. Watch how sin multiplies around a wrathful person; it grows like weeds. His rage is a permission slip for chaos everywhere.

Pride tips a man over suddenly, like overbalancing a chair. But a humble spirit—one that doesn't insist on its own way—stands firm and gains the kind of honor that lasts, because it rests on something real.

To join a thief is to become your own enemy. You take an oath before God, then you daren't testify—trapped between your oath and your crime, you destroy yourself. One wrong choice hardens you into a prisoner of your own making.

Looking back across these years, I see how often I was caught in the snare of fearing what one person might think. But readers today hear an echo here: every time I placed trust in the Lord instead of in the approval of others, I was kept safe. Not from every hardship, but from the worst captivity—the cage of other people's judgment.

Many gather at the ruler's door hoping for favor; they scheme and network and hope. But true justice? It comes from the Lord alone. He is the only judge who cannot be flattered, bribed, or swayed by appearance.

The wicked and the righteous will always repel each other because they are built for different kingdoms. This isn't meant to be hostile—it's just honest. You can't walk the same road when you're heading in opposite directions.

Agur comes forward with his name and confession—not boasting, but laying bare his ignorance before Ithiel and Ucal. There's a gentleness in a man who opens by admitting what he doesn't know. Jesus too made space for the humble to speak their doubts and questions.

"Surely I am the most ignorant man." Such a claim might sound like false modesty, but Agur isn't performing—he's genuinely small in his own eyes. That smallness is the door through which wisdom enters. The more I live, the more I see I don't know.

Agur admits he hasn't learned wisdom and doesn't know the Holy One. The confession cuts deep—not a passing thought, but the anchor of his whole address. Before we presume to teach, we must know how little we know Him. That's where all truth begins.

Five questions fired like arrows: who ascended heaven, gathers wind, binds waters, established the earth—and what is His name and His son's name? Agur points to the mystery of creation and hints at the Christ who would come. The questions themselves are the answer.

"Every word of God is flawless." Against Agur's humility stands this certainty—not about himself, but about the Almighty. His words are refined, tested, pure. When I feel small, I'm not falling into a void; I'm falling into the lap of One whose every word is true.

Don't add to His words, or He'll reprove you and call you a liar. There's a holy boundary—sacred words aren't clay to be shaped by our hands. I've seen men and women remake God's truth to fit their comfort, and it always ends in contradiction. Better to receive what is given.

"Two things I have asked of you; don't deny me before I die." Agur's prayer is urgent and bounded—he's not greedy, just clear about what matters most. The request carries the weight of finitude; we pray hardest when we know time is short.

Remove falsehood and lies; give neither poverty nor riches, but daily bread. Agur's first ask is for truth, his second for balance—not hunger that drives him to steal, not plenty that makes him forget his Maker. The prayer is as close to wisdom as a man can get.

Lest I be full and deny you, or poor and steal and dishonor your name. Agur sees clearly: prosperity can breed forgetting, want can breed sin. He asks not for ease, but for the narrow path between them—the place where a man's heart stays true. That's wisdom's bargain.

Don't slander a servant to his master, or the curse will find you. A small warning, but potent—the servant has no shield, and his voice is weak in his master's ear. To wound the defenseless is to invite the Lord's attention, not the kind we want.

A generation that curses father and doesn't bless mother—a portrait of ingratitude and willful unkindness. The parents gave life, and the children repay with curses. Jesus wept at this; He taught us to honor our mothers and fathers even at the cross.

Pure in their own eyes, yet unwashed from filth. Self-judgment is the thinnest mirror. A man can look at himself all his life and never see the mud he's wearing—only the Maker's cleansing can reveal what we truly are.

Oh, how lofty are their eyes! Their eyelids lifted up. Pride has a look—a way of turning the gaze skyward as if the world below is beneath seeing. The truly great bow their heads; the small throw theirs back.

Teeth like swords, jaws like knives—to devour the poor from the earth. Such violence is not about hunger but about appetite without conscience. The wicked don't just take; they consume with a kind of animal fury. God sees, and He judges.

The leech has two daughters: 'Give, give.' Then three things never satisfied, four that don't say enough. Greed is a living thing, always hungry, always calling for more. The image is grotesque because the reality is—some appetites have no bottom.

Sheol, barren womb, earth without water, fire—four things that never say enough. This is a meditation on yearning itself: death's pull, the ache of emptiness, thirst, heat. The Preacher knew this longing; only Christ fills the gap.

The eye that mocks father and scorns obedience to mother: ravens and eagles will pluck it out. A harsh image, but it warns: there's a judgment that comes to those who despise the ones who gave them birth. Nature herself enforces what conscience won't.

Three things too amazing, four I don't understand. Agur pivots to wonder—not the darkness of ignorance, but the bright astonishment of seeing how creation moves. There's more humility in awe than in a thousand confessions.

Eagle in air, serpent on rock, ship in sea, man with maiden—the traceless ways of living things. Each leaves no path behind; each moves by its own nature. The final pairing hints at the mystery of love, which even the wise confess they cannot fully map.

The adulterous woman eats and wipes her mouth, saying she's done no wrong. She doesn't even blush—there's no echo of conscience. It's the hardness that horrifies: the ability to consume what's forbidden and walk away unchanged.

For three things the earth trembles, four it cannot bear. The word shifts from what amazes to what shakes creation itself—disorder in the high places, chaos rising from below. Even the ground protests when righteousness is overturned.
A servant when he is king; a fool when filled with food. Power without wisdom is terror; appetite without measure is chaos. The earth knows the difference between rule and ruin.

An unloved woman when she is married; a servant who is heir to her mistress. These are the upended orders—a woman despised yet bound, a servant suddenly holding power. When stations flip without wisdom, nothing finds its place.
Four things which are little on the earth, yet exceedingly wise. Now the lens turns again—to the small, the overlooked, the ones we'd never think to learn from. Wisdom isn't always found in thrones.

Ants are not strong, yet provide their food in summer. The ant is nature's picture of faithfulness—each one plays its part, no glory sought, the work done in common. How often have I, a large thing, accomplished less than the smallest creature?

Conies are feeble folk, yet make their houses in the rocks. The coney is defenseless, but it doesn't panic—it knows where safety lives. It finds the Rock and builds there. Every small thing teaches the small man: shelter is always near if we look.

Locusts have no king, yet advance in ranks. Here's a miracle: order without a head, unity without command. How do they move as one? What tongue speaks that the whole multitude obeys? There's a mystery in it—nature knows something about harmony we've forgotten.

You can catch a lizard with your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces. The lowliest thing, catchable by a child, yet finds itself in the greatest houses. There's no place too high where the small cannot climb—and no place too dignified to find humble creatures.

Three things which are stately in their march, four stately in going. Now comes the turn to the great ones—but stateliness is not fury. It's the bearing of creatures at peace with their own nature, moving without hurry or fear.

The lion, mightiest among animals, doesn't turn away for any. There's a quietness in true strength—the lion doesn't rage to prove its power. It walks its own path, and creation yields. Might married to certainty needs no loudness.

The greyhound, the male goat, the king against whom there is no rising up. Each moves with its own bearing—swift, sure, commanding. When a king is truly just, rebellion dies before it forms. That's the power of right.

If you have done foolishly in lifting up yourself, or thought evil, put your hand over your mouth. After all these words, Agur circles back to silence—the wisest move when pride wakes or malice stirs. Sometimes the greatest word is the one we never speak.

As churning milk produces butter and wringing nose produces blood, forcing wrath produces strife. Readers today hear an echo in this—we know how easily anger ignites anger, how pressure begets pressure. The law hasn't changed: we reap what we sow, multiplied. Jesus offers a different way: gentle strength that breaks the cycle.

A king's mother—Lemuel's—had words worth preserving for all generations. What she knew, she passed to her son: that a man's character is his true crown. The deepest revelations often come not from thrones but from the quiet faithfulness of a mother's prayers.

"Oh, my son!"—a mother's cry of love layered over decades of hope and intercession. She speaks from the depth of her womb and her vows, words that hold both ache and covenant. When we pray for our children, we pray from that same sacred place.

His mother warns: don't spend yourself on seduction or ruin yourself through wrong loves. A king—a leader—must guard his strength for his true calling. Many a man has learned too late that the very thing that feels freeing becomes a yoke.

Kings are different from other men—their weakness becomes a kingdom's sorrow. A ruler's clarity must be sharp and unclouded, his judgment trusted by those under him. The vice that destroys a common man topples the throne.

If a ruler drinks and forgets the law, the afflicted are left without defense—their voices unheard, their suffering unrighted. His fog becomes their darkness. This is why a leader's sobriety is not his private business.

Yet here—something tender. Wine given to one ready to perish, to the bitter in soul: there is a place for mercy, for easing unbearable pain. The same tool that enslaves can, in proper hands and heart, bring a few hours of quiet to the dying.
To forget poverty, to remember misery no more—this is not escape, but mercy. The Scripture honors that sometimes a soul needs to set down its burden for a breath. Even God rested on the seventh day.
"Open your mouth for the mute." In ancient courts, the voiceless had no advocate but God—and those He calls to speak. A leader's first duty is to the desolate, to those the world has forgotten.

Justice for the poor and needy is the measure of a nation's righteousness. When a ruler judges with this in mind—not the rich, not the connected, but the defenseless—he mirrors the heart of God. This is what it means to judge righteously.

Now the song turns: from a mother's warning to a portrait of the woman worth finding. Her value is not in her appearance or her dowry, but in who she is—her character, her faithfulness, her fruitfulness. Worth beyond rubies.

Her husband rests in her—not because she demands trust, but because her life earns it. He lacks nothing that matters because she tends to what is real. This is the security of a marriage built on faithfulness, not on words.

"All the days of her life" — not just the honeymoon season, but the slow years of marriage, the trials, the ordinary stretches. She does him good, steady and true, through the whole arc of their years together.

Wool and flax were the work of her hands—the raw materials of every household. She doesn't just dream; she works. Her eagerness shows in her shoulders, in the hours she keeps, in the skill she builds.

She's like merchant ships—bringing goods from far away, trading, thinking beyond her own doorstep. Her vision is wide; she sees possibilities where others see only limits. Her daily work opens to the wider world.

Before anyone else wakes, she rises. She feeds her household and directs her servants with the care of a shepherd. Her work begins in darkness because her devotion doesn't wait for sunlight—it's part of who she is.

She doesn't just work—she invests. She sees a field, thinks deeply, buys it, plants a vineyard. She takes what she's earned and makes it fruitful. This is stewardship, the art of tending what God has given.

Strength is her clothing, and she makes her arms strong. This isn't brute power—it's the quiet strength of discipline and faithfulness. She doesn't break under her load; she carries it and grows capable.

She knows her work is profitable—she can see the fruit of her hands. Her lamp doesn't go out by night because the work matters to her, because she takes joy in what she's building, not just endurance.
Distaff and spindle—the tools of her trade, held steady in her hands. These were the technologies of her time, the daily craft. Her hands know their work so well they move by rhythm and memory.
She opens her arms to the poor—the same hands that work skillfully, that build and plant, reach out to those who have nothing. Her abundance doesn't make her stingy; it makes her generous.

Winter comes—scarlet clothes for warmth, provision before the hard season. She doesn't fear what's ahead because she's planned, prepared, and clothed her household against coming cold. This is the peace of readiness.

Fine linen and purple—she wears the colors of care about her own home. She doesn't neglect herself; she honors the worth of beauty and fine things. Her covering reflects both her wealth and her taste.

Her husband sits in the gates with the elders—the place where men of influence gathered to judge and speak. His honor comes because of her. A man's standing in the community often rests on the respect earned by his wife.
She makes linen garments and sells them, trades with merchants—she has a business, not just a household task. Her work produces both for her own people and for trade. She's not confined to one role.

Strength and dignity clothe her; she laughs at the time to come. Her joy isn't nervous or fragile—it's deep, rooted in knowing she's done well, that she's built something solid. Tomorrow doesn't frighten her.
When she speaks, wisdom comes—not chatter, but words that instruct and steady others. Her tongue is faithful because her life is faithful. What she says matches what she does.
She looks well to her household—watchful, present, tending to what matters. She doesn't eat the bread of idleness; she's not passive or detached. Her eyes are on her people, always.
Her children rise up and call her blessed—the highest praise. Her husband praises her too. The people closest to her, who know her best, speak her worth aloud. This is the affirmation that lasts.
"Many women do noble things, but you excel them all." Her husband's words ring in the ears of all who hear—not flattery, but recognition. She has done what few do, and he names it clearly.

Charm fades, beauty withers—we all know this truth by the time we've lived long enough. But a woman who fears the Lord, who trusts in Him and orders her life by His ways—she will be praised when the pretty faces are forgotten.

"Give her of the fruit of her hands." Readers today hear an echo in this: we see the tireless work of so many faithful women still unrecognized, their labor still often passed over in silence. Yet the song endures—still calling her to excellence, still testifying that her works praise her in the gates, whether the world watches or not.
